name: Takeko
explanation: Takeko - This name represents martial valor and bamboo-like resilience, and is often chosen by those who are born into warrior households or who are expected to uphold the family's honor through strength of character.
notes: Takeko is a real Japanese female given name. Common kanji are 武子 (martial child) or 竹子 (bamboo child). The historical Nakano Takeko (中野竹子) was a famous female warrior of the Boshin War. The explanation's references to martial valor and bamboo resilience accurately reflect these kanji meanings. The 'warrior households' framing is generic enough to work for both real Japan and L5R.

name: Fujiko
explanation: Fujiko - This name means "wisteria child". It represents grace and longevity, as the wisteria vine endures through harsh seasons and blooms with effortless beauty.
notes: Fujiko is a real Japanese female given name, written 藤子 (wisteria child). It has been used by real people, including the pen name Fujiko F. Fujio. The explanation is accurate: wisteria (fuji, 藤) is a symbol of longevity and elegance in Japanese culture, and the vine is famously long-lived. No fictional elements.

name: Masako
explanation: Masako means "elegant child" or "righteous child", which can suggest refinement in court manners or moral uprightness in the way of bushido. People with this name may be expected to serve as exemplars of propriety.
notes: Masako is a very common real Japanese female name, borne by Empress Masako (雅子, elegant child). Other kanji include 正子 (righteous child). The kanji meanings given are accurate. The reference to 'bushido' is an L5R/romanticized-Japan element, but otherwise the explanation is solid. One of the most well-attested names in this list.

name: Umeko
explanation: Umeko - This name is inspired by the natural element of the plum blossom, symbolizing beauty that opens while the snow still lies. It is often chosen for its connection to the first flowers of the year and its representation of courage, endurance and grace under hardship.
notes: Umeko is a real Japanese female name. 梅子 (plum child) is the standard writing; the famous Tsuda Umeko (津田梅子) bore this name. An alternate writing 海子 (ocean child) uses the 'umi' reading. The plum blossom symbolism (blooming in winter) is accurate and culturally significant.

name: Sadako
explanation: Sadako - A name that means "chaste and upright child", evoking the virtue of sincerity that lies at the heart of a samurai's duty to speak and act with honesty.
notes: Sadako is a real Japanese female name, written 貞子 (chaste/upright child) or 禎子. Empress Teimei's given name was Sadako. The meaning 'chaste and upright' is accurate for 貞. The 'samurai's duty' framing is generic bushido flavoring suitable for L5R. In modern pop culture the name is strongly associated with the horror film Ringu.

name: Noriko
explanation: Noriko - This name signifies a child of law and ceremony, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values propriety, the correct forms of court and a life ordered by rite.
notes: Noriko is a real Japanese female name, commonly written 典子 (child of law/ceremony) or 紀子 (child of chronicles). It is very widely used.

name: Tamiko
explanation: Tamiko - Derived from the phrase "tama no hikari", meaning the light of a jewel, this name embodies the idea of inner radiance shining outward. It is often associated with those who possess quiet dignity and a generous spirit.
notes: Tamiko is a real Japanese female name, commonly written 珠子 (jewel child) or 民子 (people's child). 'Tama no hikari' (珠の光) is a real Japanese phrase meaning 'light of a jewel.' The derivation and meaning are culturally grounded. The explanation is accurate and contains no fictional elements.

name: Tomoe
explanation: Tomoe means "swirling comma" or "the whirling crest", which can suggest the turning of water in an eddy or the heraldic mark painted on a warrior's banner. People with this name may be fierce, quick to move and hard to pin down, in the manner of a woman who rides to war.
notes: Tomoe is a real Japanese female name, written 巴. It refers to the tomoe symbol, a swirling comma-shaped design used in heraldry. The most famous bearer is Tomoe Gozen (巴御前), a legendary female warrior of the Genpei War. Also attested on a warrior-house woman (Tomoe Gozen), so it is offered to samurai as well as peasants.

name: Kameko
explanation: Kameko - This name means "tortoise child". It represents the long life and patience of the tortoise, a wish that the girl will outlast every storm.
notes: Kameko can be written 亀子 (turtle child). The turtle/tortoise is a genuine symbol of longevity in Japanese culture - the saying 'tsuru wa sennen, kame wa mannen' (cranes live a thousand years, turtles ten thousand) is a real Japanese proverb.

name: Tokiko
explanation: Tokiko - Composed of the elements "toki" meaning time or moment, and "ko" meaning child, this name symbolizes the preciousness of the present moment as taught in the Tao. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of mindfulness and awareness.
notes: Tokiko is a real Japanese female name, writable as 時子 (time child) or 登紀子. The kanji breakdown is accurate. 'The Tao' refers to the Tao of Shinsei, an L5R religious text (not the Chinese Tao Te Ching, though inspired by it). The mindfulness association is a reasonable cultural extension of the 'time/moment' meaning.

name: Chiyoko
explanation: Chiyoko - Stemming from the word "chiyo", which denotes a thousand generations, this name embodies the spirit of a line that endures. It resonates with those who are devoted to family, patient over long years and mindful of those who will come after them.
notes: Chiyoko is a real Japanese female name, written 千代子 (thousand generations child).

name: Tsukiko
explanation: Tsukiko - This name represents the moon's reflection upon still water, and is often chosen by those who are contemplative and perceptive or who are expected to bring calm clarity to moments of uncertainty.
notes: Tsukiko is a real Japanese female name, written 月子 (moon child). The moon imagery is directly tied to the kanji meaning. The 'moon's reflection on still water' is a well-known aesthetic image in Japanese culture (tsukimi, moon viewing, is a real tradition). No fictional elements in this explanation.

name: Teruko
explanation: Teruko means "shining child" or "child of illumination", which can suggest one destined to bring light to dark places or to serve as an example of virtue. People with this name may be expected to lead by moral example rather than by command.
notes: Teruko is a real Japanese female name, written 照子 (shining child) or 輝子 (radiant child). The meaning 'shining child' is accurate for the 照 kanji. The name was common in the early-to-mid 20th century. No fictional elements in this explanation.

name: Shigeko
explanation: Shigeko - A name derived from the fusion of "luxuriant" and "child", reflecting a balance between abundance and the seriousness that keeps it. It is often embraced by those who strive for a prosperous household and a daughter of real substance.
notes: Shigeko is a real Japanese female name. 茂子 (luxuriant child) and 重子 (heavy/weighty child) are both real kanji writings. The meanings given are accurate - 茂 means lush/luxuriant and 重 means heavy/important. This was a common name in earlier generations. The explanation is well-grounded with no fictional elements.

name: Okuni
explanation: Okuni - This name signifies the honored realm, the province one belongs to spoken with the respectful prefix, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values loyalty to home soil and the duty owed to the land that raised her.
notes: Okuni is a historically significant Japanese name. Izumo no Okuni (出雲阿国) founded kabuki theater in the early 1600s.

name: Fusako
explanation: Fusako can be written with two different kanji. One means "tassel child", a cluster of blossoms or a tassel on a fine cord, and the other means "whole child", all of a thing complete. The choice of kanji could reflect the family's hopes, such as a daughter who adorns the household or one who is whole and sound in body and mind.
notes: Fusako is a real Japanese female given name. Common kanji include 房子 (tassel, cluster + child) or 総子 (whole, all + child); 節子 is a different name (Setsuko) (season/fidelity child). The reading 藤子 would more typically be read 'Fujiko' rather than 'Fusako,' but the general concept of multiple kanji readings is accurate. The explanation's dual-kanji format is culturally authentic.

name: Otose
explanation: Otose - This name means "rising strength". It represents a vigor that climbs, the quiet force of a woman who keeps a house or an inn running whatever passes through its doors.
notes: Otose (お登勢) was a real historical Japanese woman - the innkeeper of the Teradaya in Fushimi who sheltered pro-Imperial samurai including Sakamoto Ryoma during the Bakumatsu period. She risked her life to protect revolutionaries working to restore imperial rule, and is remembered for her civilian courage and political loyalty.

name: Yasuko
explanation: Yasuko - This name represents tranquility and composure under pressure, and is often chosen by those who are known for their ability to remain calm in crisis or who are expected to bring peace to contentious gatherings.
notes: Yasuko (靖子, 'peaceful child' or 泰子, 'tranquil child' or 康子, 'healthy/calm child') is a very common real Japanese female given name. The meaning of tranquility and composure is accurate for all common kanji renderings. This is one of the most straightforward and authentic names in the pool.

name: Uki
explanation: Uki - This name pays tribute to the Festival of the Open Roof, an event that emphasizes gratitude for a good harvest and the joy shared under heaven when the storehouse is full. People choose this name to reflect their values for cheer, thankfulness and a household that celebrates together.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a two-mora auspicious word like the Edo register names Kiku, Matsu and Tora. Kanji 宇喜: 宇 (u, heaven, the roof of the world) + 喜 (ki, joy), read Uki; a reader parses it as joy under heaven. The kana form うき does turn up in some Edo registers outside our set, so it is probably a real commoner name even though we cannot cite it. Commoner register style, not a court name. The Festival of the Open Roof in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Ofumi
explanation: Ofumi - With origins in the legend of Ofumi the letter-writer, who kept the accounts and correspondence of an entire river town when its scribe died and taught every child on her street to read, this name evokes a sense of diligence and quiet learning. It appeals to those who admire the value of a daughter who can write.
notes: O-form: the honorific O- prefix on Fumi, an attested Edo commoner register name; the O- form is how such women were actually addressed. Kanji 文 (fumi, letters, writing, learning); the registers wrote the base name in kana. Commoner register name, not a court name. Modern association: Fumi and Fumiko remained common given names into the twentieth century. Ofumi the letter-writer in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Ino
explanation: Ino - This name pays tribute to the Well-Cleaning Festival held in the year of the boar, an event that emphasizes the stubborn labor of dredging a village well and the fresh water that rewards it. People choose this name to reflect their values for hardiness, plain persistence and the steady work that keeps a household alive.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in early-Edo name lists and in Edo village registers (1809 Kamikiyoto, 1837 Matsushima), always written in kana いの. Conventional kanji 猪 (ino, boar, also the zodiac sign) or 井 (i, well) with a kana no; girls born in a boar year were sometimes so named. Commoner register name, not a court name. The Well-Cleaning Festival in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Kinu
explanation: Kinu can be written with two different kanji. One means "silk", and the other means "garment". The choice of kanji could reflect what the family hoped for the girl, such as the fine soft wealth of silk or a life that is always well clothed and provided for.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in early-Edo name lists and in the 1733 Hatcho village register, written in kana きぬ. Conventional kanji 絹 (kinu, silk) or 衣 (kinu, garment, clothing); both are plain kun readings. Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Mine
explanation: Mine - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Girl on the Summit, in which a farmer's daughter climbed the peak above her village to light a beacon during a flood so that the boats below could find the one dry ridge. It reflects qualities such as endurance, height of purpose and a view that takes in the whole valley.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and one of the commonest in our set: early-Edo lists, Edo village registers (1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya) and late-Edo passenger lists, all in kana みね. Conventional kanji 峰 (mine, mountain peak, summit). Commoner register name, not a court name; Mine and O-Mine remained common into the Meiji era. The tale in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Kotsuru
explanation: Kotsuru - A name that means "little crane", evoking a small, graceful girl who is expected to grow into the long life and faithfulness the crane stands for.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama period name lists. Kanji 小鶴: 小 (ko, small, little) + 鶴 (tsuru, crane); the ko- prefix on a bird or auspicious word is a common pattern for women's names of that era. Commoner or low-ranking samurai household style rather than a court name. In Rokugan the crane association reads as a Crane Clan name at once, which a GM may want to use or avoid.

name: Koto
explanation: Koto chose their name in honor of the famous Kakita Koto, who played the thirteen-stringed koto before the Imperial court so beautifully that a war between two families was put off until the song ended, and then forgotten.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in the 1837 Matsushima village register and in late-Edo passenger lists, written in kana こと. Conventional kanji 琴 (koto, the thirteen-stringed zither); also plausibly 言 (koto, word). Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Ishi
explanation: Ishi - Stemming from the word "ishi", which denotes stone, this name embodies the spirit of what does not wear away. It resonates with those who are steady, unmoved by flood or fashion and relied upon by everyone around them.
notes: Attested pre-modern name with an unusually long span: Heian and Kamakura court women (Japanese Wikipedia lists of empresses and consorts), Nanbokucho court lists, Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo lists, and Edo village registers (1671 Tochii, 1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima). Kanji 石 (ishi, stone, rock); the court bearers are the -ko names 石子 read with the kun Ishi. Used at both court and commoner levels, which makes it a safe name for any caste.

name: Tane
explanation: Tane - Derived from the phrase "one seed becomes a thousand grains", this name embodies the idea of small beginnings that feed many. It is often associated with those who found households, plant orchards or teach the young.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo name lists and Edo village registers (1774 Noshio, 1837 Matsushima), written in kana たね. Conventional kanji 種 (tane, seed, lineage). Commoner register name, not a court name; the meaning carried a hope for descendants.

name: Sayo
explanation: Sayo chose their name in honor of the famous Kitsuki Sayo, who uncovered a poisoner in a provincial court by sitting silent through a whole short summer night and marking who came and went.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and very common: the late-Edo top-100, passenger lists, and Edo village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana さよ. Conventional kanji 小夜 (sa, a poetic prefix written with small + yo, night), meaning evening or night, as in sayokyoku, a nocturne. Commoner register name, not a court name. The famous Kitsuki Sayo in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Azumako
explanation: Azumako - Stemming from the word "azuma", which denotes the east and the eastern provinces, this name embodies the spirit of the sunrise frontier. It resonates with those who are restless, outward-looking and drawn to lands beyond the capital.
notes: Attested pre-modern court name: Azumako Joo, a Heian imperial princess (東子女王) on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 東子: 東 (azuma or higashi, east) + 子 (ko, child); the kun reading Azumako is the one the record gives, and the on reading would be Toshi. Court -ko name, but -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Toku
explanation: Toku - Stemming from the word "toku", which denotes virtue and merit, this name embodies the spirit of goodness that bears fruit without display. It resonates with those who are patient, morally steady and content to be judged by their deeds.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo lists, the late-Edo top-100 and passenger lists, and Edo village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima). Kanji 徳 (toku, virtue, merit), an on reading used directly as a name. Commoner register name, not a court name. Also attested on a warrior-house woman (Toku-hime, daughter of Oda Nobunaga), so it is offered to samurai as well as peasants.

name: Yayoi
explanation: Yayoi - With origins in the legend of the maiden Yayoi, who was born in the third month and each year walked the dikes of her village singing the seedlings up out of the flooded paddies, this name evokes a sense of renewal and steady increase. It appeals to those who admire the patience of late winter giving way to the rush of spring.
notes: Not attested as a personal name in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a calendar-month name given to a girl born in it. Kanji 弥生: 弥 (ya, ever more, increasingly) + 生 (oi, to grow, life), read Yayoi; this is the classical name of the third lunar month and is a real word. The reading is stylized but standard for the month. Commoner style in this setting; in modern Japan Yayoi is a common given name and also the name of an archaeological period. The maiden Yayoi in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Kesa
explanation: Kesa - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of patchwork robe-making, this name represents the monk's kesa stitched from many humble cloths into one sacred garment. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the beauty of scraps made whole and have a deep respect for the temple seamstresses who sew for the Brotherhood.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo lists, the 1774 Noshio village register and the late-Edo top-100, written in kana けさ. Conventional kanji 袈裟 (kesa, a Buddhist monk's patchwork robe), a Sanskrit loan; the name was given as a protective, Buddhist-flavored choice, and 今朝 (kesa, this morning) is the other plausible spelling. Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Omasa
explanation: The name Omasa is associated with the famous Rectification of the Rice Scales, in which a provincial magistrate ordered every merchant measure in the province checked against a single true standard and had the false ones burned in the market square. Those who choose this name try to embody values of honesty, fairness and correct dealing.
notes: O-form: the honorific O- prefix on Masa, an attested Edo commoner register name; the O- form is how such women were actually addressed. Kanji 正 (masa, correct, righteous) or 政 (masa, governance); the registers wrote the base in kana. Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Furi
explanation: The name Furi is inspired by the Swaying Bridge of the western hills, known for its long rope span that moves with every step and every wind. The name reflects the flexibility of the place and is often chosen by those who value adaptability, nerve and the ability to keep their footing when everything moves.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo lists and the 1671 Tochii village register, written in kana ふり. Conventional kanji 振 (furi, to wave, swing, sway), a plain kun reading; the register gives no kanji and the intended sense is uncertain, so treat the reading as conventional rather than certain. Commoner register name, not a court name. Also attested on a warrior-house woman (Ooku lady Furi (Ofuri no Kata), consort of Tokugawa Iemitsu), so it is offered to samurai as well as peasants.

name: Otaki
explanation: Otaki - This name pays tribute to the Waterfall Purification, a midsummer rite in which villagers stand beneath a falling stream to wash away the year's accumulated impurity before the harvest. People choose this name to reflect their values for cleansing, courage under cold water and a fresh start.
notes: O-form: the honorific O- prefix on Taki, an attested Edo commoner register name; the O- form is how such women were actually addressed. Kanji 滝 (taki, waterfall); the registers wrote the base in kana. Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Fune
explanation: Fune - This name represents a boat and is often chosen by those who are born to fishing or ferrying families or who are expected to carry others safely through rough water.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of an object name of the kind Edo commoners bore (compare Kama, Tsuchi). Kanji 舟 (fune, small boat) or 船 (fune, ship). The kana form ふね does appear as a woman's name in Edo records outside our set, so it is of a kind Edo commoner women genuinely bore (a boat is a working family's livelihood), though we have no register record of it. Commoner register style, not a court name.

name: Ofusa
explanation: Ofusa - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Tassel of Nine Sisters, in which the youngest of nine daughters wove a single tassel from a thread given by each sister so that none of them would be forgotten when they married away. It reflects qualities such as family feeling, the beauty of many gathered together and a place kept for everyone.
notes: O-form: the honorific O- prefix on Fusa, an attested Edo commoner register name; the O- form is how such women were actually addressed. Kanji 房 (fusa, tassel, cluster of fruit or flowers, also a chamber); the registers wrote the base in kana. Commoner register name, not a court name. The tale in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Tsuchi
explanation: Tsuchi - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Mallet and the Dike, in which a farm wife whose husband had been taken for the levy drove every stake of the flooded paddy dike herself with a wooden mallet through a night of rain until the water held and the village's rice was saved. It reflects qualities such as steadiness, plain endurance and a strength drawn from the soil itself.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo lists and Edo village registers (1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima), written in kana つち. Conventional kanji 土 (tsuchi, earth, soil) or 槌 (tsuchi, mallet). Commoner register name, not a court name. The tale of the Mallet and the Dike in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Hisa
explanation: Hisa can be written with two different kanji. One means "long-lasting, of long duration", and the other means "longevity, felicity". The choice of kanji could reflect what the family prayed for at her naming, such as a house that endures across the generations or a daughter who lives to see her grandchildren.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo lists, the late-Edo top-100, and Edo village registers (1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana ひさ. Conventional kanji 久 (hisa, long-lasting, of long duration); 寿 (hisa, longevity, felicity) is the other traditional spelling. Commoner register name, not a court name; Hisako is the common modern extension.

name: Masu
explanation: Masu chose their name in honor of the famous Yasuki Masu, who as rice-measurer at a Crab river port refused to shave the measuring box for the tax collector in a failed harvest year and so kept a starving town fed through the winter.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Edo village registers (1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya) and late-Edo passenger lists, where the register wrote the fuller form ますの (Masuno) in kana. Conventional kanji 益 (masu, increase, benefit) or 升 (masu, a measuring box for rice). Commoner register name, not a court name. Yasuki Masu in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Rie
explanation: Rie was a deity that was said to have granted a village its first written laws after its headman spent a winter copying sutras for her shrine.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Edo village registers (1804 Nishitomioka, 1837 Matsushima), written in the old kana りゑ. Conventional kanji 理恵 (ri, reason, principle + e, blessing, favor), the usual modern spelling; the register gives no kanji, so the choice is conventional rather than certain. Commoner register name, not a court name; Rie is a very common modern given name.

name: Koya
explanation: Koya - Derived from the phrase "a small hut, a great welcome", this name embodies the idea of hospitality that owes nothing to wealth. It is often associated with those who keep an open door on a poor road.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo lists and the 1671 Tochii village register, written in kana こや. Conventional kanji 小屋 (ko, small + ya, house, hut); 小弥 (small + ever more) is another plausible spelling and the register does not settle it. Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Toyo
explanation: Toyo was a deity that was said to have made the rice stand thick in every paddy of the Empire after a poor farmer shared his last bowl with her when she came to his door in the shape of a beggar.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and one of the commonest: early-Edo lists, the late-Edo top-100 and passenger lists, and Edo village registers (1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana とよ. Kanji 登代 (to, rise, climb + yo, generation), a standard phonetic spelling; the single character 豊 (toyo, abundant, bountiful) is the other conventional spelling and supplies the prosperity sense. Commoner register name, not a court name. The deity Toyo in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Ariko
explanation: Ariko - This name signifies presence, the plain fact of being there when one is needed, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values constancy, attendance and quiet reliability.
notes: Attested Heian and Kamakura court -ko name given here in its kun reading: 有子 (ari, to exist, to have + ko, child), on reading Yushi, borne by several Fujiwara court women. Court name; -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Some
explanation: Some - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of cloth dyeing, this name represents the moment the white silk goes into the vat and takes its color for good. It is often chosen by those who appreciate patient, layered work that cannot be undone and have a deep respect for the dyers whose hands are stained with every color but their own.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo lists, the late-Edo top-100 and the 1809 Kamikiyoto village register, written in kana そめ. Conventional kanji 染 (some, to dye), a plain kun reading; also read as the beginning of something, as in someru. Commoner register name, not a court name. Pronounced so-me, two syllables, not like the English word.

name: Sawa
explanation: Sawa - With origins in the legend of the Marsh Maiden, who guided a lost Imperial survey party through a fen by walking ahead on ground only she could see, this name evokes a sense of local wisdom, patience and hidden paths. It appeals to those who admire knowledge that comes from a place rather than a book.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo lists and Edo village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka), written in kana さわ. Conventional kanji 沢 (sawa, marsh, mountain stream). Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Onobu
explanation: The name Onobu is inspired by the Nobu Reach, a stretch of the Imperial road that runs straight for a full day's walk across a reclaimed plain, known for its unbroken line and the fields that spread out on either side of it. The name reflects the reach of the place and is often chosen by those who value steady growth, patience and ambitions that extend a little further each year.
notes: O-form: the honorific O- prefix on Nobu, an attested Edo commoner register name; the O- form is how such women were actually addressed. Kanji 伸 (nobu, to extend, to grow), the reading matching the explanation; 信 (nobu, trust, faith) is the other common spelling and the registers wrote the base in kana. Commoner register name, not a court name. The Nobu Reach in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Okichi
explanation: Okichi - Rooted in the ancient proverb "Good fortune enters only by a door that is kept open", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value hospitality, readiness and the cheerful diligence that makes room for luck.
notes: O-form: the honorific O- prefix on Kichi, an attested Edo commoner register name; the O- form is how such women were actually addressed. Kanji 吉 (kichi, good fortune, auspicious), an on reading used directly as a name. Commoner register name, not a court name. Modern association: Tojin Okichi, the historical geisha of Shimoda linked in legend to the American consul Townsend Harris. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Kuniko
explanation: Kuniko means "child of the country" or "child of the province", which can suggest a daughter raised for the realm as a whole or one whose loyalty belongs to the lands her family administers. People with this name may be dutiful, public-minded and quick to put the domain before themselves.
notes: Attested pre-modern court name: Nanbokucho and Muromachi court lists, written 國子 (the older form of 国). Kanji 國 (kuni, country, province) + 子 (ko, child), kun reading Kuniko; the on reading would be Kokushi. Court -ko name, but -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting; Kuniko was also a common twentieth-century given name.

name: Sono
explanation: The name Sono is inspired by the Garden of the Nine Pines, known for its walled orchards and paths raked fresh every dawn. The name reflects the ordered abundance of the place and is often chosen by those who value cultivation, patience and beauty that is tended rather than found.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: the late-Edo top-100 and passenger lists, and Edo village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana その. Conventional kanji 園 (sono, garden, orchard). Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Kunishi
explanation: Kunishi - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A realm is held together by its smallest households", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value civic loyalty, order and belonging to something larger than a village.
notes: Attested pre-modern court name given here in its on reading: 邦子内親王, a Kamakura imperial princess on Japanese Wikipedia's list of empresses. Kanji 邦 (ho, kuni, country, realm) + 子 (shi, child); the kun reading is Kuniko, and the on reading Kunishi is a mixed reading (kun for 邦, on for 子) of the kind conventionally used for court women's -ko names. Court name; -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Kusu
explanation: The name Kusu is associated with the famous Planting of the Camphor Groves, in which the governor of a coastal province ordered camphor trees set along every road after a typhoon had stripped the land bare, so that the trees stood for centuries after their planters were gone. Those who choose this name try to embody values of foresight, patience and work done for descendants one will never meet.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo lists and Edo village registers (1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana くす. Conventional kanji 楠 (kusu, camphor tree) or the phonetic 久寿 (ku, long-lasting + su, longevity). Commoner register name, not a court name. The Planting of the Camphor Groves in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Shimo
explanation: Shimo can be written with two different kanji. One means "frost", and the other means "below". The choice of kanji could reflect the circumstances of the birth, such as a girl born on the first frosty morning of autumn or the youngest daughter of a lower household.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: early-Edo lists, the late-Edo top-100 and passenger lists, and Edo village registers (1671 Tochii, 1774 Noshio), written in kana しも. Conventional kanji 霜 (shimo, frost) or 下 (shimo, below, lower). Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Tsune
explanation: Tsune can be written with two different kanji. One means "usual, everyday", and the other means "perpetual, unchanging". The choice of kanji could reflect which kind of constancy the family had in mind, such as a woman who is the same in famine and in feast or one whose word given once holds for life.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and one of the commonest: early-Edo lists, the late-Edo top-100 and passenger lists, and Edo village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana つね. Conventional kanji 常 (tsune, constant, usual, everyday); 恒 (tsune, perpetual, unchanging) is the other traditional spelling. Commoner register name, not a court name; also a common element in samurai men's nanori (Tsunemoto, Tsunenaga).

name: Chikako
explanation: Chikako - A name that means "child of closeness", evoking a daughter who stays near, the warmth of kin and a household that keeps no distance among its own.
notes: Attested pre-modern court name: Nanbokucho and Muromachi court lists, written 親子. Kanji 親 (chika, intimate, close; also oya, parent) + 子 (ko, child), kun reading Chikako; the on reading would be Shinshi. Court -ko name, but -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting; Chikako is also a familiar modern given name.

name: Tomi
explanation: Tomi - Derived from the phrase "wealth is a full granary and a full house", this name embodies the idea of prosperity measured in rice and children rather than coin. It is often associated with those who manage a household well and make a little go a long way.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: the late-Edo top-100 and passenger lists, and Edo village registers (1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima), where the register wrote the fuller form とみへ (Tomie) in kana. Conventional kanji 富 (tomi, wealth, abundance). Commoner register name, not a court name.

name: San
explanation: San was a deity that was said to have set heaven, earth and humanity in their three levels after the world had been a single formless mist with no above or below.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and among the very commonest: early-Edo lists, the late-Edo top-100, and Edo village registers (1671 Tochii, 1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1825 Kano, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana さん. Conventional kanji 三 (san, three), often given to a third daughter. Commoner register name, not a court name. Note that san is also the everyday honorific suffix, so Osan was the usual form of address. The deity San in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Oshige
explanation: Oshige - This name means "luxuriant, thriving". It represents a field gone thick and green, a household that grows from little and the vigor of a woman whose work makes everything around her flourish.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Shige, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Shige is how such a woman was actually addressed. Conventional kanji 茂 (shige, "luxuriant, thriving"), a plain kun reading. A commoner register name, not a court name.

name: Okuma
explanation: Okuma - This name is inspired by the natural element of the bear of the mountain forests, symbolizing rough-hewn strength and the fierce protectiveness of a mother for her cubs. It is often chosen for its connection to the deep woods and their winter stillness and its representation of courage, endurance and loyalty that asks nothing in return.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Kuma, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Kuma is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 熊 (kuma, "bear"), a plain kun reading; animal names of this kind were common among Edo villagers. A commoner register name. Unrelated to the modern surname Okuma (大隈), which uses different characters.

name: Kuno
explanation: Kuno - Stemming from the word "hisashii", which denotes something long-lasting and enduring, this name embodies the spirit of constancy through the years. It resonates with those who are steady, patient, and slow to change their loyalties.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in late-Edo village registers (1804 Nishitomioka, 1825 Kano), where it was written in kana as くの. The most conventional kanji spelling is 久乃 (ku "long-lasting, enduring" + the phonetic 乃 no), the standard form for register names ending in -no. A commoner register name.

name: Satoko
explanation: Satoko - Composed of the elements "village, hometown" and "child", this name symbolizes a daughter of the home fields, rooted in the land her family has always worked. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of belonging, loyalty to kin and the comfort of familiar places.
notes: Attested court name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of court women. Kanji 里子, read in its kun form Satoko; the on-reading is Rishi. 里 means "village, hometown" and 子 is the standard feminine "child" suffix. A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste. In modern Japanese the same characters also spell the common noun satogo, "foster child", which readers may notice.

name: Nabe
explanation: Nabe - This name signifies the cooking pot at the center of the hearth, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values a full household, plain generosity and the warmth of a meal shared with whoever comes to the door.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo name lists and in the 1671 Tochii village register. Kanji 鍋 (nabe, "cooking pot"), a plain kun reading; household-object names of this kind were normal for commoner women. A commoner register name.

name: Nobuko
explanation: Nobuko - A name that means "child of trust", evoking a daughter whose word can bear weight and a household known for its kept promises.
notes: Attested court name: borne by Heian empresses and imperial consorts on Japanese Wikipedia and listed among Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) court women. Kanji 信子, read in its kun form Nobuko; the on-reading is Shinshi. 信 means "faith, trust, sincerity" and 子 is the feminine suffix. A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste. Nobuko was a very common given name in twentieth-century Japan.

name: Koboshi
explanation: Koboshi - This name represents a little acolyte, the small child who sweeps the temple steps, and is often chosen by those who are raised near a shrine or monastery or who are expected to serve the Fortunes with humble, cheerful labor.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of commoner women, recorded as 小法師女, that is "the woman Koboshi", with 女 marking her sex rather than forming part of the name. Kanji 小法師 (koboshi, "little priest, young acolyte"), read with its ordinary readings; it began as an affectionate nickname of the kind medieval commoners bore. A commoner name, not a court name.

name: Sue
explanation: The name Sue is associated with the famous Last Rice of the Long Drought, in which a river town's headwoman divided the final storehouse among every household by count of mouths, youngest first, so that the last-born were fed before the harvest failed and the rains at last returned. Those who choose this name try to embody values of fairness to the smallest, endurance to the end of a hard season, and care for the last child of a full house.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and one of the most common of all: appears in early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, passenger lists, and village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana as すへ or すゑ. Conventional kanji 末 (sue, "end, last"), a plain kun reading, with 季 (sue, "youngest, last-born") the other traditional spelling; it was commonly given to a youngest daughter. A commoner register name. Its resemblance to the English name Sue is coincidental. The Last Rice of the Long Drought is a Rokugani invention for the explanation.

name: Saru
explanation: Saru can be written with two different kanji. One means "monkey", and the other means "to go away". The choice of kanji could reflect what the family wanted the name to do, such as wishing the child the monkey's nimble cleverness or charming illness to depart from her.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in the 1564 Sugaura register and in early-Edo name lists, written both in kana (さる) and as 猿. Kanji 猿 (saru, "monkey"), a plain kun reading; the name was also chosen for its pun on saru "to depart", so that illness would leave the child. A commoner register name.

name: Tsunako
explanation: Tsunako - A name derived from the fusion of "to bind, to hold together" and "child", reflecting a balance between the cords that hold a household fast and the daughter who must both tie them and be tied by them. It is often embraced by those who strive for unity, proper conduct and loyalties that do not slip.
notes: Attested court name: borne by a late-Edo imperial consort, Konoe Tsunako (近衛維子), on Japanese Wikipedia's lists of empresses and consorts. Given name 維子, read in its kun form Tsunako (the same name is also read Koreko); the on-reading is Ishi. 維 means "to bind, to hold together" and 子 is the feminine suffix; the alternative spelling 綱子 uses 綱 "rope, principal cord". A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste.

name: Juna
explanation: The name Juna is inspired by the Juna Springs, a hot spring in the hills known for its waters that are said to add a year of life for every night spent bathing in them. The name reflects the gentle longevity of the place and is often chosen by those who value endurance, good health and a gracefulness that outlasts hardship.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a two-mora name built on an auspicious element, like the Edo register names Kiku and Tora. Kanji 寿奈 (ju "long life, felicity" + the phonetic 奈 na), both ordinary readings; be aware the -na ending sounds more modern than most register names. A commoner-style name. The Juna Springs in the explanation are a Rokugani invention.

name: Tama
explanation: Tama - A name that means "jewel", evoking something small, precious, and polished by care until it shines.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo name lists, passenger lists, and village registers (1774 Noshio, 1825 Kano). Kanji 玉 (tama, "jewel, gem, ball"), a plain kun reading. A commoner register name. Tama is also the stock name for a pet cat in Japan. Also attested on a warrior-house woman (Hosokawa Tama (Gracia), daughter of Akechi Mitsuhide), so it is offered to samurai as well as peasants.

name: Tora
explanation: Tora chose their name in honor of the famous Matsu Tora, who held a mountain ford alone for a night and a day against raiders so that her village's rice could be carried to safety behind her.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and one of the most common: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, passenger lists, and village registers (1671 Tochii, 1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1809 Kamikiyoto), written in kana (とら) and as 虎. Kanji 虎 (tora, "tiger"), a plain kun reading; the tiger was an auspicious guardian animal for girls. A commoner register name.

name: Yae
explanation: Yae was a deity that was said to have folded the mountain cherry's petals eight times over after a mortal gardener wept that one thin layer of blossom was too little beauty for so short a spring.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: late-Edo village registers (1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya) record it in kana as やゑの (Yaeno), of which Yae is the base form. Conventional kanji 八重 (yae, "eightfold, many-layered", as in double-flowered blossoms), a standard kun reading. A commoner register name. Niijima Yae, the Bakumatsu-era defender of Aizu, is a famous historical bearer.

name: Muneko
explanation: Muneko - Derived from the phrase "carry on the line", this name embodies the idea of a daughter as the keeper of her ancestors' way. It is often associated with those who tend the family shrine, remember the old names, and hold the household to its founding vows.
notes: Attested court name: borne by a Heian empress on Japanese Wikipedia's list of empresses and listed among Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) court women. Kanji 宗子, read in its kun form Muneko; the on-reading is Soshi. 宗 means "lineage, ancestral line, sect" and 子 is the feminine suffix. A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste.

name: Motoko
explanation: Motoko - Composed of the elements "endowment" and "child", this name symbolizes a daughter born with every gift her house could provide. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of natural talent, good resources, and a foundation on which greatness can be built.
notes: Attested court name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of court women. Kanji 資子, read Motoko; the on-reading is Shishi. 資 means "resources, endowment, capital" and 子 is the feminine suffix; moto is a nanori (name-only) reading of 資, so this is a stylized reading of the kind court names often carry. A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste. Modern bearers usually write Motoko as 素子 or 元子, as with Kusanagi Motoko of Ghost in the Shell.

name: Mume
explanation: Mume - This name signifies the plum that flowers while snow still lies on the ground, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values fortitude, early courage and beauty that arrives before the thaw.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and one of the most common: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, passenger lists, and village registers (1804 Nishitomioka, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya). Kanji 梅 ("plum"); mume is the older pronunciation of ume, preserved in the registers, so the reading is archaic rather than stylized. A commoner register name.

name: Tsuruo
explanation: Tsuruo - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The crane lives a thousand years", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value longevity, dignified bearing, and fidelity to a single mate for life.
notes: Attested court name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of court women. Kanji 鶴王 (tsuru "crane" + o "king, sovereign"), both ordinary readings; the -o (王) suffix was a genuine medieval naming element for court women alongside -ko, and it reads oddly to modern ears, so flag it as archaic. A court name; in this setting the style suits any caste.

name: Oyoshi
explanation: Oyoshi - With origins in the legend of Yoshi of the Lucky Ferry, who is said to have rowed a Fortune disguised as a beggar across a flooded river for no fee and was repaid with a lifetime of good catches, this name evokes a sense of good fortune earned through kindness. It appeals to those who admire generosity that expects nothing back.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Yoshi, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Yoshi is how such a woman was actually addressed. Conventional kanji 吉 (yoshi, "good luck, auspicious"), a standard kun reading, though 良 "good" was also used. A commoner register name.

name: Chise
explanation: Chise - This name pays tribute to the Festival of the Thousand Shallows, an event that emphasizes the thanksgiving of the river villages each late summer, when the water drops low enough to ford at every crossing and neighbors on either bank can visit at last. People choose this name to reflect their values for persistence, neighborliness and the many small crossings a life is made of.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in passenger lists and the 1837 Matsushima village register, written in kana as ちせ. Conventional kanji 千瀬 (chi "thousand" + se "shallows, rapids"), both ordinary kun readings. A commoner register name. Hatori Chise of The Ancient Magus' Bride is a modern pop-culture bearer. The Festival of the Thousand Shallows in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Okame
explanation: Okame means "tortoise" or, by long custom, "ten thousand years", which can suggest the slow creature itself or the longevity it has always stood for. People with this name may be patient, steady and impossible to hurry.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Kame, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Kame is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 亀 (kame, "tortoise"), a plain kun reading; the tortoise is the emblem of longevity. A commoner register name. Okame is also the name of the round-cheeked comic mask of Japanese folk theater (also called Otafuku), a real association any Japanese reader would make.

name: Kura
explanation: The name Kura is associated with the famous Levy of the Sealed Storehouses, in which a provincial governor refused to open the granaries to a corrupt tax collector's men until the Emperor's own seal arrived, and was vindicated when the collector's warrant proved forged. Those who choose this name try to embody values of prudence, stewardship, and firmness in guarding what has been entrusted to them.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, and village registers (1671 Tochii, 1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana as くら. Conventional kanji 倉 (kura, "storehouse, granary"), a plain kun reading; a wish that the house never lack stores. A commoner register name.

name: Enyo
explanation: The name Enyo is inspired by the Temple of Ten Thousand Threads in the eastern hills, known for its cords of red silk that pilgrims tie between the pillars to mark the bonds they owe to others. The name reflects the connectedness of the place and is often chosen by those who value loyalty, obligation honestly kept, and the ties that hold a village together.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a Buddhist-flavored two-character name mixing an on-reading with a kun-reading, of the kind temple-raised girls sometimes bore. Kanji 縁世 (en "karmic bond, connection" + yo "world, generation"), both ordinary readings, though the combination is unusual and should be treated as stylized. A commoner-style name.

name: Ochiyo
explanation: Ochiyo - This name represents a thousand generations and is often chosen by those who are the daughters of long-established farming houses or who are expected to carry the family line forward for ages to come.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Chiyo, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Chiyo is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 千代 (chi "thousand" + yo "generations, ages"), both ordinary kun readings. A commoner register name.

name: Sukeko
explanation: Sukeko - This name means "helping child". It represents a daughter raised to be her family's support, the one who steadies the household when others falter.
notes: Attested court name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of court women. Kanji 相子, read Sukeko; the on-reading is Soshi. 相 means "to aid, a minister; mutual" and 子 is the feminine suffix; suke is a nanori (name-only) reading of 相, so flag it as a stylized court reading. A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste.

name: Itoko
explanation: Itoko means "thread" or "beloved", which can suggest the fine silk a household spins or the tender word a parent uses for a cherished child. People with this name may be delicate, dear to those around them, and quietly essential to the pattern of a family.
notes: Attested name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of court women and in Azuchi-Momoyama name lists, recorded as いと子. Conventional kanji 糸子 (ito "thread" + the feminine suffix 子), a plain kun reading; the pun on itoshi "beloved" is traditional. A court -ko name that later appears among samurai households; in this setting -ko suits any caste. The name is a homophone of itoko, "cousin", which Japanese readers notice.

name: Oyuki
explanation: Oyuki - Stemming from the word "yuki", which denotes snow, this name embodies the spirit of a quiet, clean beginning. It resonates with those who are calm, pure-hearted and unhurried.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Yuki, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Yuki is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 雪 (yuki, "snow") is the conventional spelling, with 幸 (yuki, "happiness, good fortune") the traditional alternative; both are standard kun readings. A commoner register name. Oyuki is also the snow-woman of the Yuki-onna ghost tale as told by Lafcadio Hearn.

name: Naka
explanation: Naka chose their name in honor of the famous Ide Naka, who settled a forty-year feud between two villages by seating both headmen at her own table and refusing to pour the tea until they had clasped hands.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and among the most common: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, passenger lists, and the 1837 Matsushima register, written in kana as なか. The most conventional kanji is 仲 (naka, "relations, harmony between parties"), with 中 (naka, "middle", for a middle daughter) an equally traditional spelling. A commoner register name. Ide Naka in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Miya
explanation: Miya can be written with two different kanji. One means "shrine, palace", and the other is a phonetic pairing meaning "beautiful" and "ever more". The choice of kanji could reflect the family's intent, such as placing a child under the protection of the shrine or simply wishing her a beauty that grows.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo lists and village registers (1671 Tochii, 1733 Hatcho, 1804 Nishitomioka), written in kana (みや) and as 宮. Kanji 宮 (miya, "shrine, palace"), a plain kun reading; the phonetic 美弥 (mi, beautiful + ya, ever more) is a later alternative spelling. A commoner register name.

name: Chima
explanation: Chima was a deity that was said to have scattered a thousand true words across the Empire after a lying magistrate's speech caused a river to run backward.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Azuchi-Momoyama and early-Edo name lists, written in kana as ちま. The registers give no kanji; the most conventional reconstruction is 千真 (chi "thousand" + ma "truth"), both ordinary readings, but treat the spelling as a plausible reconstruction rather than a recorded one. A commoner register name.

name: Osato
explanation: Osato - Derived from the phrase "the village of one's birth", this name embodies the idea of home as the place one carries everywhere. It is often associated with those who stay close to their kin, welcome strangers as guests, and never forget the road back.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Sato, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Sato is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 里 (sato, "village, hometown"), a plain kun reading. A commoner register name.

name: Okin
explanation: Okin - A name that means "gold", evoking a daughter treasured like coin in a household that has little else of worth.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Kin, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Kin is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 金 (kin, "gold, money"), its ordinary on-reading, which is how the register name was read. A commoner register name.

name: Yone
explanation: Yone can be written with two different kanji. One means "rice", and the other is a phonetic pairing meaning "to give" and "root". The choice of kanji could reflect what the family saw in the name, such as the grain that feeds the Empire or a gift that puts down roots in the household.
notes: Attested pre-modern name and among the most common: appears in early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, passenger lists, and village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana (よね) and as 米. Kanji 米 (yone, "rice"), the older kun reading of the character that survives in names; the phonetic 与根 (yo, to give + ne, root) is an alternative register spelling. A commoner register name.

name: Saki
explanation: Saki - Stemming from the word "saku", which denotes blossoming, this name embodies the spirit of a flower opening at its proper hour. It resonates with those who are lively, hopeful, and quick to brighten a room.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in early-Edo lists, a late-Edo top-100 compilation, and village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1774 Noshio, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1837 Matsushima), written in kana as さき. The most conventional kanji is 咲 (saki, "to bloom"), a standard name reading; 先 (saki, "ahead, first") is a traditional alternative. A commoner register name. Saki is a very common modern given name.

name: Otsuya
explanation: Otsuya - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A lacquer bowl shines only after the hundredth polishing", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value patience, refinement and a grace that is earned by slow work rather than given.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Tsuya, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Tsuya is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 艶 (tsuya, "gloss, luster, charm"), a plain kun reading. A commoner register name. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Okiku
explanation: Okiku - This name is inspired by the natural element of the chrysanthemum, symbolizing a bloom that opens late in the year and lasts when other flowers have gone. It is often chosen for its connection to the frost-touched gardens of the ninth month and its representation of patience, endurance and a dignity that ripens with age rather than fading.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Kiku, an attested Edo commoner name found in village registers; O-Kiku is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 菊 (kiku, "chrysanthemum"), its ordinary on-reading. A commoner register name. Okiku is also the wronged servant of the ghost story Bancho Sarayashiki, who counts plates from a well, a real association most Japanese readers know.

name: Omatsu
explanation: Omatsu - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of bonsai, this name represents the pine trained for decades into a shape that looks like a mountain's own work. It is often chosen by those who appreciate patience measured in generations and have a deep respect for gardeners whose trees outlive them.
notes: The honorific O- prefix on Matsu, an attested Edo commoner name and one of the most common; O-Matsu is how such a woman was actually addressed. Kanji 松 (matsu, "pine"), a plain kun reading; the pine stands for constancy and long life. A commoner register name.

name: Beniya
explanation: The name Beniya is associated with the famous Crimson Harvest, in which the safflower fields of a northern province bloomed so richly one year that the dye paid off a decade of the domain's debts, and the daimyo remitted the villages' taxes in thanks. Those who choose this name try to embody values of industry, shared prosperity, and beauty that also feeds a household.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a dye or color name joined to the -ya ending seen in register names like Tsuya. Kanji 紅弥 (beni "safflower red, rouge" + 弥 ya "ever more, increasingly"), both ordinary readings, though the combination is stylized; be aware that 紅屋 (Beniya) is the far more usual parse, a rouge-seller's shop name. A commoner-style name.

name: Iyako
explanation: Iyako means "child of ever more" or "child of increase", which can suggest a household hoping each year will outdo the last or a daughter meant to grow in every virtue. People with this name may be ambitious, generous and never quite content with enough.
notes: Attested court name: appears in a Nanboku-cho (Muromachi) list of court women. Kanji 彌子, read Iyako, using the old form 彌 of modern 弥; the on-reading is Bishi. 彌 means "ever more, increasingly" (kun reading iya, as in iyamasu) and 子 is the feminine suffix; the kun reading is genuine but unfamiliar to modern readers, so flag it as archaic. A court -ko name; in this setting -ko suits any caste.

name: Shina
explanation: Shina - This name represents grace and refinement of bearing and is often chosen by those who are raised to carry themselves with quiet dignity or who are expected to bring good manners and good standing to the family they marry into.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in early-Edo lists and late-Edo village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1809 Kamikiyoto, 1837 Matsushima, 1848 Hakkenya), written in kana as しな. Conventional kanji 品 (shina, "grace, refinement, quality"), a plain kun reading. A commoner register name.

name: Hanako
explanation: Hanako - This name represents the flower in full bloom and is often chosen by those who are raised for the courts of the Crane or who are expected to bring beauty and grace to whatever house they marry into.
notes: This name follows the attested Heian court pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子 read in kun-yomi; the same women were recorded in on-yomi (e.g. 定子 Teishi/Sadako). I do not know of a specific Heian court woman recorded as 華子, so treat the name as pattern-attested rather than individually attested. Kanji 華子: 華 (hana, flower, splendor) + 子 (ko, child); the reading is regular kun-yomi. Caste: samurai and court style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting. Modern association: one of the most common twentieth-century Japanese girls' names, usually written 花子.

name: Yukiko
explanation: Yukiko - This name means "child of good fortune". It represents the blessing a family hopes the Fortunes have laid on a daughter, and the luck she is expected to carry into her husband's house.
notes: This name follows the attested Heian court pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子 read in kun-yomi; the same women were recorded in on-yomi (e.g. 定子 Teishi/Sadako). I do not know of a specific Heian court woman recorded as 幸子, so treat it as pattern-attested rather than individually attested; the on-reading would be Koshi. Kanji 幸子: 幸 (yuki, fortune, happiness) + 子 (ko, child); the kun reading yuki for 幸 is regular in names. Caste: samurai and court style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting. Modern association: extremely common in the twentieth century, though today usually parsed as 雪子 (snow).

name: Kimiko
explanation: Kimiko means "child of the lord" or "noble child", which can suggest a daughter of high birth or a girl expected to carry herself with a lord's dignity. People with this name may be proud, formal and keenly aware of rank.
notes: This name follows the attested Heian court pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子 read in kun-yomi; the same women were recorded in on-yomi (e.g. 定子 Teishi/Sadako). Kimiko 君子 is itself attested on Heian court women (on-reading Kunshi). Kanji 君子: 君 (kimi, lord, sovereign) + 子 (ko, child); regular kun-yomi. Note that 君子 read kunshi is also the Confucian term for the gentleman of virtue, which lends the name a second layer. Caste: samurai and court style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Ieko
explanation: Ieko - A name derived from the fusion of "house, household" and "child", reflecting a balance between the line that must continue and the daughter who carries it forward. It is often embraced by those who strive for filial duty, continuity and a household kept whole.
notes: This name follows the attested Heian court pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子 read in kun-yomi; the same women were recorded in on-yomi (e.g. 定子 Teishi/Sadako). Ieko 家子 is itself attested on Heian court women (on-reading Kashi). Kanji 家子: 家 (ie, house, household) + 子 (ko, child); regular kun-yomi. Caste: samurai and court style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Kiyoko
explanation: Kiyoko - This name signifies purity and clarity of heart, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values honesty, cleanliness before the kami and a life free of stain.
notes: This name follows the attested Heian court pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子 read in kun-yomi; the same women were recorded in on-yomi (e.g. 定子 Teishi/Sadako). Kiyoko 清子 is itself attested on Heian court women (on-reading Seishi). Kanji 清子: 清 (kiyo, pure, clear) + 子 (ko, child); regular kun-yomi. Caste: samurai and court style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting. Modern association: a common twentieth-century name; the modern Kiyoko is usually the same 清子.

name: Nagako
explanation: Nagako - A name that means "child of long life", evoking the wish that a daughter outlive her parents and see the household prosper through many seasons.
notes: This name follows the attested Heian court pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子 read in kun-yomi; the same women were recorded in on-yomi (e.g. 定子 Teishi/Sadako). Nagako 長子 is itself attested on Heian court women (on-reading Choshi). Kanji 長子: 長 (naga, long, hence long life) + 子 (ko, child); regular kun-yomi, though a reader may also parse 長子 as choshi, eldest child. Caste: samurai and court style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting. Modern association: Empress Kojun, consort of the Showa Emperor, was born Kuni Nagako 良子 with a different first kanji.

name: Koreko
explanation: Koreko was a deity that was said to have judged the quarrels of the first villages after the Fortunes withdrew to the heavens, and every ruling she gave was found to be right.
notes: This name follows the attested Heian court pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子 read in kun-yomi; the same women were recorded in on-yomi (e.g. 定子 Teishi/Sadako). I am not certain of a specific Heian court woman recorded as 是子, so treat the name as pattern-attested rather than individually attested; the on-reading would be Zeshi. Kanji 是子: 是 (kore, this, right, correct) + 子 (ko, child); kore is the regular kun reading and the name sense is rightness. Caste: samurai and court style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting. No notable modern bearers; the name is essentially archaic today.

name: Katako
explanation: Katako - Derived from the phrase "a wise child knows the house", this name embodies the idea of a daughter whose good sense holds the household together. It is often associated with those who counsel their lords quietly and well.
notes: This name follows the attested Heian court pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子 read in kun-yomi; the same women were recorded in on-yomi (e.g. 定子 Teishi/Sadako). Katako 賢子 is itself attested on Heian court women (on-reading Kenshi, notably a daughter of Murasaki Shikibu). Kanji 賢子: 賢 (kata, wise, virtuous) + 子 (ko, child); kata is an archaic kun reading of 賢, historically attested but unusual to a modern eye, so flag it as a stylized reading. Caste: samurai and court style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Naoko
explanation: Naoko - Composed of the elements "honest, upright" and "child", this name symbolizes a daughter who cannot be bent from the truth. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of honesty, candor and a straight heart.
notes: This name follows the attested Heian court pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子 read in kun-yomi; the same women were recorded in on-yomi (e.g. 定子 Teishi/Sadako). Naoko 直子 is itself attested on Heian court women (on-reading Jikishi or Chokushi). Kanji 直子: 直 (nao, honest, straight, upright) + 子 (ko, child); regular kun-yomi. Caste: samurai and court style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting. Modern association: a very common twentieth-century name, still written 直子.

name: Tomoko
explanation: Tomoko - Rooted in the ancient proverb "to know is the beginning of the Way", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value learning, discernment and the counsel of the Tao.
notes: This name follows the attested Heian court pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子 read in kun-yomi; the same women were recorded in on-yomi (e.g. 定子 Teishi/Sadako). I do not know of a specific Heian court woman recorded as 知子, so treat it as pattern-attested rather than individually attested; the on-reading would be Chishi. Kanji 知子: 知 (tomo, knowing, wisdom) + 子 (ko, child); tomo is a name-reading (nanori) of 知 rather than its everyday kun-yomi, so flag it as slightly stylized. Caste: samurai and court style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting. Modern association: among the most common girls' names of the postwar decades, usually written 智子.

name: Riyo
explanation: Riyo - Stemming from the word "ri", which denotes reason and the proper order of things, this name embodies the spirit of a household kept in balance across the generations. It resonates with those who are level-headed, fair in their dealings and slow to be swayed by rumor.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Edo village registers (1733 Hatcho, 1804 Nishitomioka, 1809 Kamikiyoto) and in early-Edo name lists, and ranks in the late-Edo top-100 compilation; the registers wrote it in kana. The conventional kanji are 理代, ri (reason, principle) plus yo (generation, era). A commoner register name, though -ko-less two-mora names of this shape were borne across castes.

name: Gin
explanation: Gin - Stemming from the word "gin", which denotes silver, this name embodies the spirit of quiet worth that does not need to glitter like gold. It resonates with those who are steady, modest and valued more the longer they are known.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in Edo village registers (1774 Noshio, 1848 Hakkenya), in early-Edo name lists and among Sengoku-era women; the registers wrote it in kana. The conventional kanji is 銀, gin (silver), the on reading. A commoner register name of the single-word type, like Kiku or Matsu.

name: Kise
explanation: Kise - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of kimono dressing, in which layers of silk are set one over another until the whole reads as a single graceful line, this name represents joy shown to the world through careful presentation. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the harmony of color and season and have a deep respect for the dressers and dyers whose hands are never seen in the finished figure.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (1804 Nishitomioka) and ranks in the late-Edo top-100 compilation; the register wrote it in kana. The conventional kanji are 喜世, ki (joy) plus se (world, generation); the sound also echoes kise-ru, to dress someone, which the explanation plays on. A commoner register name.

name: Yaya
explanation: Yaya can be written with two different kanji. One means "ever more" written twice, and the other means "eight" written twice, a number held auspicious for the way its strokes widen as they fall. The choice of kanji could reflect the family's hope, such as growth that keeps on growing like a rice shoot in the sixth month or a fortune that spreads wider with each year.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in early-Edo and Azuchi-Momoyama name lists; recorded in kana. The conventional kanji is the reduplicated 弥々, ya (ever more, increasingly, as in iya-masu) written once and then with the repetition mark, a stylized but standard way of writing such names; the phonetic 八々 (ya, eight, doubled) is an alternative spelling. A commoner name; in modern Japanese yaya means slightly and yaya-ko a baby, both unrelated to the name.

name: Kachiko
explanation: Kachiko - With origins in the legend of the Empress of the Garden, who was said to have planted a grove of trees with her own hands and then founded a temple beneath them for the poor, this name evokes a sense of beauty joined to wisdom and generosity. It appeals to those who admire a grace that builds something lasting rather than merely adorning a court.
notes: Attested pre-modern court name: Tachibana no Kachiko (橘嘉智子, 786-850), empress consort of Emperor Saga and founder of Danrin-ji, listed among the imperial consorts on Japanese Wikipedia. The kanji are 嘉 (excellent, auspicious), 智 (wisdom) and 子 (child); the reading Kachiko is the one recorded for her, and each character is read in its plain on or kun form. A court name of the Heian type, three characters ending in -ko. The historical Kachiko was also called the Danrin Empress and is the model for the explanation above.

name: Ako
explanation: Ako - Stemming from the word "ako", which denotes "my child", this name embodies the spirit of a parent's tenderness spoken aloud every time the girl is called. It resonates with those who are warm, unguarded and secure in being loved.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Azuchi-Momoyama name list with the kanji 吾子, a (I, my) plus ko (child), literally "my child", an old term of endearment that became a given name. The reading is the plain kun reading of both characters. A commoner name, though the -ko ending suits any caste in this setting. Unrelated to Ako (赤穂), the castle town of the famous forty-seven ronin.

name: Muku
explanation: Muku - A name derived from the fusion of "nothing" and "stain", reflecting a balance between the emptiness the Tao prizes and the spotless conduct the Fortunes reward. It is often embraced by those who strive for purity of intent without pride in it.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Azuchi-Momoyama name list without kanji. The most conventional spelling is 無垢, mu (nothing) plus ku (dirt, stain), the ordinary word for unblemished or innocent, read in its standard on readings; an alternative is 椋, the muku tree (Aphananthe aspera), a plant name of the kind Edo commoners bore. A commoner name.

name: Chiki
explanation: Chiki - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the tea ceremony, in which a single bowl is served with a thousand small courtesies, this name represents a thousand joys gathered into one quiet hour. It is often chosen by those who appreciate stillness and exactness and have a deep respect for the tea masters who make a lifetime of practice look effortless.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an early-Edo name list, recorded in kana. The conventional kanji are 千喜, chi (thousand) plus ki (joy), both in standard readings. A commoner register name of the two-character auspicious type.

name: Mutsu
explanation: The name Mutsu is associated with the famous Accord of the Six Villages, in which six feuding hamlets along one river agreed under a magistrate's seal to share their irrigation water by turns rather than by force. Those who choose this name try to embody values of harmony, neighborly good faith and the patience to settle a quarrel by talking.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an early-Edo name list, recorded in kana. The conventional kanji is 睦, mutsu (harmony, friendly intimacy, as in mutsumajii), a standard kun reading; the name is unrelated to Mutsu province (陸奥), which uses different characters. A commoner register name. Modern association: the battleship Mutsu and the Mutsu region of northern Japan, both from the province name rather than this kanji.

name: Yoso
explanation: The name Yoso is inspired by the far frontier villages beyond the last post-station, known for their hard winters and for taking in whoever arrives on the road. The name reflects the openness of such distant places and is often chosen by those who value hospitality to strangers and a willingness to leave home for a new beginning.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an early-Edo name list, recorded in kana. There is no fixed kanji; the sound is the common word yoso (elsewhere, another place, written 余所 or 他所), which the explanation draws on, and register names of this shape were usually written phonetically, e.g. 与曽 (give, formerly) as ateji with no meaning of its own. A commoner register name.

name: Urako
explanation: Urako - This name represents the bay and its sheltered shore and is often chosen by those who are born to coastal families or who are expected to be a safe harbor for everyone around them.
notes: Attested pre-modern court name: appears in a Nanbokucho-period list of court women with the kanji 浦子, ura (bay, inlet, seashore) plus ko (child); the on reading would be Hoshi, the kun reading Urako. A court name of the medieval -ko type. Not to be confused with the common noun urako (an unrelated modern usage is rare).

name: Tsugi
explanation: Tsugi - This name pays tribute to the Festival of Succession, an event that emphasizes each household naming its heir before the ancestors' tablets on the first morning of the new year. People choose this name to reflect their values for continuity, duty to ancestors and the quiet work of keeping a line alive.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (1774 Noshio), recorded in kana. The conventional kanji is 継, tsugi (to succeed, to carry on, as in ato-tsugi, an heir), a standard kun reading; 次 (next) is an equally plausible spelling for a daughter born after another child. A commoner register name. The Festival of Succession in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Hata
explanation: Hata chose her name in honor of the famous Crane weaver Asahina Hata, who wove a single bolt of silk so fine that the daimyo hung it in place of a painted screen and made her the first commoner ever named a treasure of the province.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (1774 Noshio), recorded in kana. The conventional kanji is 機, hata (a loom, as in hata-ori, weaving), a standard kun reading; 旗 (banner) is the other common spelling of the same sound. A commoner register name of the object type. The Asahina weaver in the explanation is invented, and the sound also matches the historical Hata (秦) immigrant clan of ancient Japan, which is unrelated.

name: Noe
explanation: Noe - With origins in the legend of Noe of the River Fields, who dug the first channel from a sluggish inlet out across a dry plain and turned it into paddy that fed a province, this name evokes a sense of plenty and rootedness. It appeals to those who admire quiet labor that changes the land for good.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (1809 Kamikiyoto), written in historical kana as のゑ with the old character we (ゑ), read Noe. The conventional kanji are 野江, no (field) plus e (inlet, river branch), both standard kun readings; 乃恵 (blessing) is a common alternative. A commoner register name. Noe of the River Fields in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Kima
