explanation: Kima - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Honest Seamstress, in which a village girl found a purse of gold in a torn sleeve she was mending and walked three days to return it to its owner, who was so moved that he adopted her as his heir. It reflects qualities such as honesty, joy in plain work and trust in the Fortunes to reward the right thing.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (1690 Goromaru), recorded in kana. The conventional kanji are 喜真, ki (joy) plus ma (truth, genuine), both standard readings; the register spelling gives no kanji, so this is a plausible reconstruction rather than a recorded one. A commoner register name. The tale in the explanation is invented.

name: Tsuyo
explanation: Tsuyo - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Reed and the Flood, in which a village girl lashed herself to the reeds of the riverbank when the spring flood came and bent with the water all night, and was found alive at dawn where the pines had been torn up by the roots. It reflects qualities such as endurance, resilience and the strength to outlast trouble rather than to fight it.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Edo village register (1733 Hatcho), recorded in kana. The conventional kanji is 強, tsuyo (strong, the stem of tsuyoi), a standard kun reading. A commoner register name of the virtue-word type, the female counterpart of names like Take. The tale of the Reed and the Flood in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Mare
explanation: Mare - With origins in the legend of the Once-Born Crane, a bird said to appear only once in a hundred years over a village that would prosper, this name evokes a sense of rarity, wonder and being singled out by the heavens. It appeals to those who admire the extraordinary and believe their daughter was a gift not to be expected twice.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an early-Edo name list, recorded in kana. The conventional kanji is 稀, mare (rare, uncommon), a standard kun reading; 希 is a common alternative. A commoner register name, often given to a child born late or after long waiting. The legend in the explanation is invented.

name: Gonko
explanation: Gonko - Stemming from the word "gon", which denotes authority and the right to act in another's name, this name embodies the spirit of a woman trusted to speak for her house. It resonates with those who are capable, discreet and comfortable holding power on behalf of someone else.
notes: Attested pre-modern court name: appears in a Nanbokucho-period list of court women with the kanji 權子, the old form of 権 (authority, power; also provisional or acting, as in the office title gon-no-kami) plus 子 (child); the on reading is Gonshi, with Gonko the kun-style reading given here. A court name of the medieval -ko type. Rare in modern Japan and with no notable modern bearer.

name: Fukuju
explanation: Fukuju - This name is inspired by the natural element of the fukuju-so, the golden flower that opens through the last snow at the turn of the year, symbolizing good fortune and long life arriving together. It is often chosen for its connection to the New Year and its representation of prosperity, endurance and hope that outlasts the winter.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in a Nanbokucho-period list of commoner women as 福寿女, fuku (good fortune) plus ju (long life) with the suffix 女 (woman), a marker medieval records attached to female commoners' names; the given name proper is Fukuju, both characters in standard on readings. A commoner name of the auspicious-word type, and the word fukuju also names the New Year flower Adonis ramosa, which the explanation uses.

name: Konabe
explanation: Konabe - A name derived from the fusion of "small" and "cooking pot", reflecting a balance between humility and the daily nourishment that keeps a household alive. It is often embraced by those who strive for usefulness and warmth rather than grandeur.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an Azuchi-Momoyama name list without kanji. The conventional spelling is 小鍋, ko (small) plus nabe (pot, pan), both standard kun readings; household-object names of this kind were genuinely borne by women of the period. A commoner name.

name: Run
explanation: Run - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of lacquerware, in which coat after coat is laid down and left to stay until the surface holds for a hundred years, this name represents what remains when patience is finished. It is often chosen by those who appreciate durability over show and have a deep respect for the craftsmen who let time do half the work.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: appears in an early-Edo name list and in an Edo village register (1804 Nishitomioka), recorded in kana as るん. There is no conventional kanji: names ending in n were written phonetically, most often 留ん, ru (to stay, to remain) plus the kana n, and the explanation draws on that character; the reading is therefore partly kana and should be flagged as unusual. A commoner register name.

name: Junko
explanation: Junko - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The river that keeps to its banks is the one that reaches the sea", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value obedience, due order and gentleness in victory.
notes: Court name following the attested Heian pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子: 順子 was borne by Fujiwara no Junshi (Nobuko, 809-871), consort of Emperor Ninmyo, and Junko is the kun-style reading of the same characters, with Junshi the on reading. The kanji are 順 (obedient, gentle, in due order) and 子 (child). A court name; -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting. Modern association: Junko is one of the most common twentieth-century Japanese female names, so it reads as familiar rather than archaic. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Rinko
explanation: Rinko - A name derived from the fusion of "ethics" and "child", reflecting a balance between the strict proper relations of lord and retainer and the tenderness owed to a daughter. It is often embraced by those who strive for propriety without coldness.
notes: Court name following the attested Heian pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子: 倫子 was borne by Minamoto no Rinshi (964-1053), the principal wife of Fujiwara no Michinaga, and Rinko is the kun-style reading of the same characters, with Rinshi the on reading. The kanji are 倫 (ethics, morals, proper human relations) and 子 (child). A court name; -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Uta
explanation: Uta - A name that means "song", evoking the poems sung at festivals, the planting songs of the paddies and a voice that lifts everyone within hearing.
notes: Not in the tagged registers for this batch but a genuine Edo commoner name (うた appears in period registers elsewhere), so it is kept as an attested rather than invented entry. The conventional kanji is 歌, uta (song, poem), a standard kun reading; 詩 (poem) is an alternative. A commoner register name of the single-word type. Modern association: still a common given name, and the sound is the same as in waka poetry.

name: Wasa
explanation: Wasa chose her name in honor of the famous Crane courtier Doji Wasa, who ended a year-long dispute between two great houses by seating their lords at one tea gathering and refusing to let either leave before the other had bowed.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of the two-mora kana names of Edo village registers, and the sound わさ does occur as a commoner name in the period, so it may well be attested elsewhere. The conventional kanji are 和佐, wa (harmony, peace) plus sa (to assist), both standard readings, though such names were usually written phonetically. A commoner-style name; the Doji Wasa of the explanation is invented.

name: Zenko
explanation: Zenko - A name that means "child of goodness", evoking a daughter who gives her own bowl to a stranger's child without being told to.
notes: Plausible pre-modern name following the attested Heian court pattern of an auspicious kanji plus 子 (-ko), but we have no record of this specific name being borne by a historical person. Kanji 善子: 善 'goodness, virtue' (zen, the on reading) + 子 'child' (ko); the Heian scholarly convention would read it Zenshi, so Zenko mixes an on reading with kun ko, which is common in later usage. Court/samurai style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Zuiko
explanation: Zuiko - Derived from the phrase "a sign of good fortune", this name embodies the idea of a child who arrives as a blessing already foretold. It is often associated with those who are born under a favorable omen or into a season of plenty.
notes: Plausible pre-modern name following the attested Heian court pattern of an auspicious kanji plus 子 (-ko), but we have no record of this specific name being borne by a historical person. Kanji 瑞子: 瑞 'auspicious omen, felicitous sign' (zui, on reading) + 子 'child' (ko); Heian court convention would read it Zuishi. Court/samurai style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Jueiko
explanation: Jueiko - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A long life is the root, and honor is the flower", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value endurance first and glory only as its natural fruit.
notes: Plausible pre-modern name following the attested Heian court pattern of two auspicious kanji plus 子 (-ko), but we have no record of this specific name being borne by a historical person. Kanji 寿栄子: 寿 'longevity, long life' (ju) + 栄 'glory, flourishing' (ei) + 子 'child' (ko), all on readings except ko; a three-kanji -ko name is rarer than the two-kanji form and the reading is somewhat stylized. Court/samurai style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Eijuko
explanation: Eijuko - This name represents glory and long life and is often chosen by those who are born into houses that expect much of them or who are expected to carry a family's honor well into old age.
notes: Plausible pre-modern name following the attested Heian court pattern of two auspicious kanji plus 子 (-ko), but we have no record of this specific name being borne by a historical person. Kanji 栄寿子: 栄 'glory, flourishing' (ei) + 寿 'longevity' (ju) + 子 'child' (ko), on readings except ko; a three-kanji -ko name is rarer than the two-kanji form and the reading is somewhat stylized. Court/samurai style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting.

name: Mitsuko
explanation: Mitsuko - A name that means "child of light", evoking a lantern kept burning through a long winter night so that no one feels forgotten.
notes: This name follows the attested Heian court pattern of one auspicious kanji plus 子 read in kun-yomi; the same women were recorded in on-yomi (e.g. 定子 Teishi/Sadako). Mitsuko 光子 is itself attested on Heian court women (on-reading Koshi). Kanji 光子: 光 (mitsu, light, radiance) + 子 (ko, child); regular kun-yomi. Caste: samurai and court style, though -ko is acceptable for any caste in this setting. Modern association: in physics 光子 read koshi is the word for photon, a coincidence that is occasionally the subject of jokes about the name.

name: Ritsu
explanation: Ritsu - With origins in the legend of Ritsu the Measurer, a village woman who kept her rice measure so honest that a magistrate made it the standard for the whole county, this name evokes a sense of fairness, order and quiet integrity. It appeals to those who admire a life kept in careful measure.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in Edo village registers (1774 Noshio, 1804 Nishitomioka), where it was recorded in kana as りつ. The conventional kanji is 律 (ritsu, "law, rule, measure", also the word for a musical mode), read with its ordinary on-reading. A commoner register name for women, not a court -ko form. In modern Japan Ritsu is a unisex given name and is familiar from the manga and anime K-On! (Tainaka Ritsu). The register gives no kanji. Ritsu the Measurer in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Joko
explanation: Joko - This name signifies purity, a child kept as clear of the world's mud as a mountain spring, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values clean hands, honest speech and a heart with nothing hidden in it.
notes: Not recorded on any historical person in our sources; the name is built on the attested Heian and Kamakura court pattern of an auspicious kanji plus 子, and is plausible under that pattern even though we have no record of a specific bearer named Joko. Written 浄子: 浄 (jō, "pure, clean") plus 子 (ko, "child"), read with the on-reading of 浄 as court -ko names usually were. A court-style name in this setting, though -ko may be borne by any caste. No notable modern association; 浄 is common in Buddhist vocabulary (as in Jōdo, the Pure Land).

name: Wakiko
explanation: Wakiko - A name derived from the fusion of "harmony" and "nobility", reflecting a balance between the peace that yields and the rank that must not. It is often embraced by those who strive for a dignity that makes friends rather than enemies.
notes: Not recorded on any historical person in our sources; the name follows the attested Heian court pattern of auspicious kanji plus 子 and is plausible under it, but we have no record of a specific historical Wakiko. Written 和貴子: 和 (wa, "harmony, peace"), 貴 (ki, "noble, precious") and 子 (ko, "child"). The three-kanji shape is slightly fuller than the usual two-kanji court name but each reading is standard. A court-style name in this setting; -ko is acceptable for any caste. No notable modern association.

name: Kou
explanation: Kou - This name pays tribute to the Sweeping of the Doorsteps, a village observance on the last evening of the year, an event that emphasizes order, gratitude and the good fortune that enters a tidy house. People choose this name to reflect their values for diligence, a welcome kept ready and luck earned rather than begged for.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: appears in an Azuchi-Momoyama period name list and in the 1837 Matsushima village register, recorded in kana as こう. The conventional kanji is 幸 (kō, "good fortune, happiness"); other spellings such as 香 ("fragrance") were also used for this sound, so the register gives no way to choose between them. A commoner register name for women, not a court -ko form. In modern Japan the name is more familiar in its extended forms (Kōko, Kōichi); Kou itself is now rare. The Sweeping of the Doorsteps in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Beniko
explanation: Beniko - Stemming from the word "beni", which denotes the crimson dye pressed from safflower petals, this name embodies the spirit of vivid, unfading color. It resonates with those who are striking, warm and unwilling to fade into a crowd.

A -ko name in the court style, acceptable for any caste in this setting. Beniko is a real but uncommon modern given name.

name: Goma
explanation: The name Goma is associated with the famous Sesame Tithe of the Lean Years, in which a river province whose rice had failed paid its tax in pressed sesame oil, and the Emperor, rather than punish the shortfall, ordered the oil burned in every shrine lamp of the capital in the province's honor. name: Zusa

name: Ranno

name: Itoe
explanation: The name Itoe is associated with the famous Weaving of the Flood Nets, in which the women of a river town spun every thread they owned into nets that held back the driftwood of a great flood. Those who choose this name try to embody values of cooperation, practical devotion and strength made from many small strands.
notes: Built on an attested naming mechanism (a stem + 江 e, the same stem-plus-suffix pattern Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno); plausible under that pattern, but we have no record of this specific name ever being borne. 糸 (ito, thread) + 江 (e, inlet) reads Itoe. name: Nene
explanation: The name Nene is associated with the famous Peace of the Twice-Sworn Oath, in which the wife of a rising general held his home province together through his long campaigns and, when two of his captains fell out, made each swear peace twice - once before her and once before the other. Those who choose this name try to embody values of steadiness at home and the patient repair of quarrels.
notes: 寧 (nei/ne, peace) with the repetition mark 々 gives Nene; the kanji spelling is a later convention, since her name was written in kana. Commoner register style, not a court name. name: Nobue
explanation: The name Nobue is inspired by the Inlet of Trust, a sheltered harbor on the Crane coast, known for its water that stays calm when the open sea is running high and for merchants who seal their bargains there with a word rather than a written note. The name reflects the reliability of the place and is often chosen by those who value promises kept and a calm that can be counted on.

explanation: Chiyozuru - A name derived from the fusion of "a thousand generations" and "crane", reflecting a balance between the long patience of a lineage and the grace of a single life within it. It is often embraced by those who strive for a legacy that outlasts them.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Chiyozuru, a Kamakura-period woman on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 千代鶴 (thousand + generation + crane), read chi-yo-zuru with the usual voicing of tsuru in compound; both halves are stock auspicious elements. Elite or samurai-daughter style in this period; the crane element also appears in Edo commoner registers as Tsuru.

name: Hori
explanation: Hori - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of garden-making, this name represents the moat or channel that a master cuts to bring living water through stone and moss. It is often chosen by those who appreciate the patient shaping of a landscape and have a deep respect for gardeners who make water seem to have always flowed where it flows.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Horibe Hori (b. 1675), samurai daughter of the Ako domain, on Japanese Wikipedia; the source records the name in kana ほり. Conventional kanji 堀 (moat, dug channel), read hori, kun reading; as a girl's name it is an everyday word used as a name, which was normal. Samurai-daughter style here, though the plain-word form is indistinguishable from a commoner register name.

name: Hite
explanation: The name Hite is inspired by the terraces of the eastern hill country, known for their fields that catch the first light before the valley wakes. The name reflects the bright, early-rising character of the place and is often chosen by those who value diligence and a clear head at dawn.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: recorded once among the 112 women who took refuge at the Mantokuji divorce temple in Kozuke (Ueno Kazuo et al., Namae to shakai, Waseda UP 2006, via Kishimoto). The register wrote it in kana ひて; this is almost certainly the unvoiced register spelling of Hide, conventional kanji 秀 (to excel, outstanding), so the reading is stylized by the register's habit of dropping voicing marks. Odd-looking but genuinely recorded; commoner register style.

name: Hiru
explanation: Hiru - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the Noon Bride, in which a farmer's daughter who was born at midday refused to conduct any business after dark, and so was the only one in her village never cheated by the fox-spirits who bargain by lamplight. It reflects qualities such as openness, plain dealing and a life lived with nothing hidden.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: listed by Kishimoto as an uncommon Edo commoner name that had largely vanished by Meiji; the underlying register is not named, and the name is rare, so use sparingly. Recorded in kana ひる; conventional kanji 昼 (daytime, noon), read hiru, kun reading; an everyday word as a name. Odd-looking but genuinely recorded; commoner register style. The tale of the Noon Bride in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Hochi
explanation: Hochi means "guarded wisdom" or "wisdom that protects", which can suggest a mind kept carefully or a knowledge used to shelter others. People with this name may be discreet, deliberate, and trusted with what must not be said aloud.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Shinohara Hochi (b. 1595), early-Edo samurai woman, on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 保智 (protect, keep + wisdom), on-yomi ho + chi, a conventional two-character compound. Samurai-daughter style; on-yomi two-character names of this kind were an elite register, not a village one.

name: Hangaku
explanation: Hangaku - Composed of the elements "board" and "tablet", this name symbolizes a name carved plainly on a signboard for all to read and held against anyone who would tear it down. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of blunt courage and a reputation that can hold a wall.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Hangaku Gozen, the Kamakura-period warrior woman of the Jo clan who held a fortress against the shogunate in 1201, on Japanese Wikipedia. Her name is written both 板額 (board + tablet or frame) and 坂額 (slope + tablet), read han-gaku, on-yomi in both. Warrior-family style, and famous enough that a Rokugani bearer would be read as invoking a martial heroine. Hangaku appears in ukiyo-e and in modern games as one of the archetypal onna-bugeisha.

name: Iroha
explanation: Iroha was a deity that was said to have taught the first letters of the syllabary to mortals after she was born to parents who had prepared only a son's name and had to read it anew for a daughter.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Irohahime (1594-1661), eldest daughter of Date Masamune, on English Wikipedia. Her kanji are 五郎八 (five + son + eight), a boy's name chosen before her birth in expectation of a son; the reading iroha is entirely stylized, taken from the first three syllables of the iroha poem rather than from the characters (which would read Gorohachi). If used in Rokugan, explain the reading in prose or simply write it in kana. Daimyo-family style. The deity of the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Acha
explanation: Acha - Composed of the elements "the affectionate prefix a-" and "tea", this name symbolizes a girl small and warm enough to be called by a pet name, and the cup that is offered before any hard talk begins. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of easy familiarity and the kind of hospitality that settles a dispute.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Lady Acha (Acha no Tsubone, 1555-1637), concubine of Tokugawa Ieyasu and his envoy at the Osaka peace talks, on English Wikipedia. Kanji 阿茶 (the affectionate prefix a- + tea), read a-cha; the prefix character carries no meaning beyond endearment, so the name is essentially a pet form of Cha. Samurai or court style.

name: Yamabuki
explanation: Yamabuki - This name is inspired by the natural element of the kerria, the yellow rose that spills down mountainsides in spring, symbolizing golden brightness on rough ground. It is often chosen for its connection to the hill slopes where the flower grows wild and its representation of cheer that needs no tending.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Yamabuki Gozen, Heian-period consort of Minamoto no Yoshinaka, on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 山吹 (mountain + blow), read yama-buki, kun reading; as a compound it is the name of the kerria, the yellow spring rose, not a literal mountain wind. Court or warrior-household style in the source; flower names were also common in Edo commoner registers. Yamabuki is also the Japanese color word for that golden yellow.

name: Yonoko
explanation: Yonoko - Composed of the elements "leisure" and "open field", this name symbolizes a life with room to breathe, the child of a household that has enough and to spare. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of ease and untroubled abundance.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Udono Yonoko, a late-Edo woman on Japanese Wikipedia (the surname is stripped here). Kanji 余野子 (surplus, leisure + field + child), read yo-no-ko; reading is the standard one for this bearer, confirm on the article. Late-Edo elite or literate-household style; -ko is fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Yayoko
explanation: Yayoko - A name derived from the fusion of "ever more" and "the world", reflecting a balance between a hope that keeps growing and the generations it must be patient with. It is often embraced by those who strive for a life that leaves the world a little wider than they found it.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Kuwabara Yayoko, a late-Edo woman on Japanese Wikipedia (surname stripped); the source spells the given name やよ子, kana plus the -ko character. Conventional kanji 弥世子 (ever more + world, generation + child), read ya-yo-ko without strain; the kana may equally stand for 弥生 (yayoi, the third month and spring growth), which would make the reading stylized. Late-Edo literate-household style; -ko is fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Nui
explanation: Nui - Stemming from the word "sewing", which denotes the joining of cloth with needle and thread, this name embodies the spirit of mending what is torn and holding a household together seam by seam. It resonates with those who are patient, deft, and quietly indispensable.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: one of the 19 most frequent women's names (together over a quarter of 2,942 entries) in the shumon-ninbetsu-cho of Umaji village, Tanba, for 1837, 1846, 1854 and 1865 (Jugaku and Kabashima 1958, as quoted in Mori 2024). The register wrote it in kana ぬい; conventional kanji 縫 (to sew), read nui, kun reading, an everyday craft word as a name. Commoner register style at its most typical.

name: Noro
explanation: Noro - This name is inspired by the natural element of dew on an open field, symbolizing the brief brightness that comes with every dawn and is gone by the time the household is at work. It is often chosen for its connection to the morning meadow and its representation of freshness, modesty and things valued precisely because they do not last.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: listed by Kishimoto as an uncommon Edo commoner name that had largely vanished by Meiji; the underlying register is not named, and the name is rare, so use sparingly. Recorded in kana のろ; conventional kanji 野露 (field + dew), read no-ro with the on reading of 露, which is the ordinary reading in compounds. Odd-looking to a modern ear (noro also means 'slow'), but genuinely recorded; commoner register style.

name: Wiro
explanation: The name Wiro is associated with the famous Cutting of the Long Channel, in which the farmers of three quarreling villages dug a single irrigation channel from one spring across all their fields in a single dry season, and no village went hungry that year. Those who choose this name try to embody values of shared labor and water carried to every field, not only one's own.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: cited by Kishimoto (after Tsunoda Bunei) as a name that appeared suddenly in late Edo and mostly died out without passing into Meiji; no place given, and it is rare. Recorded in kana ゐろ with the historical kana wi, so the modern reading is Iro; conventional kanji 井路 (well + road), read i-ro, a real word for an irrigation channel. Odd-looking but genuinely recorded; commoner register style. The Cutting of the Long Channel in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Miki
explanation: Miki - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of bonsai, this name represents the trunk, the one part of the tree that every branch depends on and that the artist shapes slowest of all. It is often chosen by those who appreciate strength that is not showy and have a deep respect for cultivators who think in decades.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: cited by Kishimoto as the overwhelmingly common two-mora type across registers from Ezo to Kyushu, and also borne by named late-Edo women on Japanese Wikipedia. Registers wrote it in kana みき; conventional kanji 幹 (trunk, main stem), read miki, kun reading; modern bearers usually take 美樹 or 美紀 instead. Commoner register style, fine for any caste. Miki is a very common modern woman's name.

name: Kaku
explanation: The name Kaku is associated with the famous Flight of the Thousand Cranes, in which a river town's every household folded and released paper cranes on the same morning to mark a peace between two feuding families, and the sky over the ford went white. Those who choose this name try to embody values of reconciliation and the long life that peace makes possible.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: recorded once among the 112 women who took refuge at the Mantokuji divorce temple in Kozuke (Ueno Kazuo et al., Namae to shakai, Waseda UP 2006, via Kishimoto). The register wrote it in kana かく; the conventional kanji here is 鶴 (crane) in its on reading kaku, a sister form to the common register name Tsuru, though the kana could also stand for 覚 (awakening) or 角 (corner). Commoner register style.

name: Mon
explanation: The name Mon is inspired by the Gate of Crests in the old capital, known for the hundreds of family emblems carved into its lintels by every house that ever swore service there. The name reflects the enduring loyalty of the place and is often chosen by those who value belonging to something with a mark and a memory.
notes: Attested late-Edo commoner name: recorded once among the 112 women who took refuge at the Mantokuji divorce temple in Kozuke (Ueno Kazuo et al., Namae to shakai, Waseda UP 2006, via Kishimoto). The register wrote it in kana もん; conventional kanji 紋 (crest, pattern), read mon, on reading and the ordinary word; 門 (gate) is the other everyday reading of the same sound. Commoner register style; very short names of this kind were normal in Edo villages.

name: Tsumaki
explanation: Tsumaki - This name signifies the hem of a robe, the edge that is turned and stitched so that the whole garment holds, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values care for the unseen parts of a household and work that is only noticed when it is left undone.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Otsumaki, a Sengoku-period woman on Japanese Wikipedia, with the honorific o- stripped; the source records the name in katakana ツマキ. Conventional kanji 褄 (the hem or skirt of a kimono) plus 木, or as one word 妻木 (wife + tree, also a surname), read tsuma-ki; neither spelling is attested for this bearer. Samurai-household style, though the O- form is how such women were addressed in any caste.

name: Kameju
explanation: Kameju - This name represents the long life of the tortoise and is often chosen by those who are born to a house that has lost children before, or who are expected to outlive every trouble that comes for them.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Shimazu Kameju (1571-1630), daughter of Shimazu Yoshihisa, on English and Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 亀寿 (tortoise + longevity), read kame-ju, a kun-on mix that was normal for elite girls' names of the period; both characters are stock auspicious elements. Daimyo-family style; the tortoise element also appears alone as Kame in Edo commoner registers.

name: Mego
explanation: Mego - This name means "love". It represents the affection a household pours into a child it has waited for, and the hope that she will be as cherished in the house she marries into as in the one that named her.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Megohime (1568-1653), wife of Date Masamune, on English and Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 愛 (love, affection); the reading mego is stylized, a Tohoku pet form of the character's kun reading (megu-mu, to cherish) rather than the ordinary ai, so a Rokugani bearer should have it explained or take a northern-dialect flavor. Daimyo-family style.

name: Tazu
explanation: Tazu - This name is inspired by the natural element of the crane standing in the flooded paddies, symbolizing long life and watchfulness. It is often chosen for its connection to the rice fields at planting time and its representation of grace that does not stray far from home.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Otazu no Kata, a Sengoku-period samurai woman on English and Japanese Wikipedia, with the honorific o- stripped. Kanji 田鶴 (paddy field + crane), read ta-zu, a classical poetic word for the crane in which the second character's reading is compressed; the reading is conventional for this word. Samurai-household style; Tazu also appears as a commoner name in Edo registers.

name: Kametsuru
explanation: Kametsuru - This name is inspired by the natural element of the tortoise and the crane, the two creatures of longevity, symbolizing a life as long as both of theirs together. It is often chosen for its connection to the still ponds and marsh edges where the two are seen side by side and its representation of patience paired with grace.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Kametsuruhime (b. 1613), of a daimyo family, on Japanese Wikipedia. Her kanji are 亀鶴 (tortoise + crane), the two classic emblems of long life paired, read kame-tsuru. Daimyo-family style; both elements also appear singly in commoner registers.

name: Minami
explanation: Minami - This name signifies the south, the direction of warmth, the noon sun and the sea road, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values openness, generosity and a face turned toward the light.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Shimazu Ominami (b. 1511), a Sengoku-period samurai woman on Japanese Wikipedia, with the honorific o- stripped. Kanji 南 (south), read minami, kun reading; a plain direction word as a name. Samurai-household style in the source; the same plain-word pattern is common in commoner registers. Minami is a common modern given name for both sexes.

name: Tokiwa
explanation: Tokiwa - A name that means "everlasting rock", evoking the pine on the crag that keeps its green through every winter, and a constancy that outlasts the seasons.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Tokiwa Gozen (b. 1138), mother of Minamoto no Yoshitsune, on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 常盤 (always + broad rock), read toki-wa, the classical word for something evergreen and unchanging; the reading is standard though not a simple sum of the characters' ordinary readings. Court or warrior-household style. Tokiwa Gozen is a fixture of the Heike tales and of noh and kabuki.

name: Senzuru
explanation: Senzuru - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A thousand cranes are folded one at a time", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value patience, devotion and great work done in small pieces.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Senzuru Gozen, a Heian-period woman on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 千鶴 (thousand + crane), which the modern reader would read Chizuru; sen-zuru mixes the on reading of 千 with the voiced kun reading of 鶴, a period reading that is unusual today and should count as stylized. Court or warrior-household style. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Komori
explanation: Komori - A name derived from the fusion of "small" and "grove", reflecting a balance between modest size and the shelter a wood gives. It is often embraced by those who strive for a quiet strength that hides more than it shows.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Komori Gozen (d. 1189), a Heian-period woman on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 小森 (small + grove, forest), read ko-mori, kun reading, a plain landscape word that is also a common surname. Court or warrior-household style. Modern ears may hear komori as 'babysitter' (子守) or 'bat' (蝙蝠).

name: Mitsugi
explanation: Mitsugi - Derived from the phrase "the first rice goes to the lord", this name embodies the idea of tribute freely rendered, the portion that is offered before the household eats. It is often associated with those who serve without being asked and give before they are owed.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Toyota Mitsugi (1774-1829), late-Edo religious leader executed for founding a heterodox sect, on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 貢 (tribute, offering), read mitsugi, kun reading; a single-character word name. Commoner in origin, though the source is a Wikipedia biography rather than a village register; the character reads as commoner or merchant style.

name: Kumako
explanation: Kumako - Composed of the elements "bear" and "child", this name symbolizes a strength that protects its own, the mother bear's fierceness given to a daughter. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of hardiness, warmth, and a temper best not tested.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Ikeda Kumako, a late-Edo woman on Japanese Wikipedia (surname stripped). Kanji 熊子 (bear + child), read kuma-ko, kun reading, straightforward. Late-Edo elite or literate-household style; animal-strength names like Kuma and Tora also appear in Edo commoner registers, and -ko is fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Tsukubako
explanation: Tsukubako - Rooted in the ancient proverb "The mountain that opens its door is never lonely", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value hospitality, humility and the reward of an open door.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Toki Tsukubako, a late-Edo woman on Japanese Wikipedia (surname stripped), named for Mount Tsukuba. Kanji 筑波子 (Tsukuba, written build + wave, + child), read tsukuba-ko; the mountain name is a place name whose characters are not read for meaning, so the proverb in the explanation draws on the mountain's legend from the Hitachi fudoki rather than on the characters; the proverb itself is a Rokugani invention. Late-Edo literate-household style; -ko is fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Koman
explanation: Koman - Rooted in the ancient proverb "a small coin kept is ten thousand earned", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value thrift, patience and the slow building of a household's fortune.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Seki no Koman (b. 1767), a late-Edo commoner woman (a teahouse keeper at the Seki post station) on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 小万 (small + ten thousand), read ko-man; Man alone was a common Edo register name and ko- is a diminutive prefix, so this is a commoner form. Commoner style; the name also belongs to several kabuki heroines, which is how most modern readers meet it.

name: Otomae
explanation: Otomae - With origins in the legend of a road-side singer who taught the songs of the common road to an Emperor's retired court until the grandest hall in the land rang with the tunes of ferrymen and packhorse drivers, this name evokes a sense of art without rank. It appeals to those who admire talent that rises from nowhere and is honored for what it is.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Otomae (1085-1169), the imayo singer who taught Emperor Go-Shirakawa, on Japanese Wikipedia; the explanation follows her real story. Kanji 乙前 (second, younger + before, front), read oto-mae, both kun readings; a name in the entertainer register, likely a stage name. Hinin or entertainer-caste style in Rokugani terms rather than court or village.

name: Kitsuno
explanation: Kitsuno - Stemming from the word "good fortune", which denotes luck that arrives as a blessing rather than a reward, this name embodies the spirit of a household touched by the Fortunes. It resonates with those who are lucky, cheerful, and generous with what came to them freely.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Kitsuno (d. 1566), concubine of Oda Nobunaga and mother of Nobutada, on English Wikipedia. Kanji 吉乃 (good luck, auspicious + the particle no as a name-ender), read kitsu-no; the on reading kitsu for 吉 is conventional in names though kichi is the commoner word reading. Samurai-household style; the -no ending is also frequent in Edo commoner registers.

name: Kaji
explanation: Kaji - This name is inspired by the natural element of the paper-mulberry tree, symbolizing the leaf on which wishes are written at the Star Festival and the bark that becomes paper. It is often chosen for its connection to the riverside groves and its representation of eloquence, wishes made and words that last.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Okaji no Kata (1578-1642), concubine of Tokugawa Ieyasu, on English Wikipedia, with the honorific o- stripped. Kanji 梶 (paper mulberry; the same character also means an oar or rudder), read kaji, kun reading. Samurai-household style; a plain tree name of the kind commoner registers also carry. Kaji leaves are still the traditional writing surface for Tanabata wishes.

name: Onami
explanation: Onami - A name derived from the fusion of "gentle" and "south", reflecting a balance between a soft manner and the warm, sunward direction it faces. It is often embraced by those who strive for a kindness that has a definite direction and does not drift.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Onamihime (1541-1602), sister of Date Terumune and a Sengoku power in her own right, on English Wikipedia. Kanji 阿南 (the affectionate prefix 阿 + south), read o-nami, where 阿 takes the reading o rather than the usual a and 南 its ordinary kun reading; note this is on-ami, not the honorific o- on a name Nami, so the prefix is part of the name and should not be stripped. Daimyo-family style.

name: Shoju
explanation: Shoju - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A long life begins with a good omen and is kept by good conduct", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value auspicious beginnings and the steady living that earns an old age.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Shojuhime, a Heian-period woman on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 祥寿 (auspicious, good omen + longevity), read sho-ju, on-yomi in both, a conventional elite compound. Court style; two-character on-yomi names like this were an aristocratic register, not a village one. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Teruhi
explanation: Teruhi - This name is inspired by the natural element of the shining sun on the day the clouds finally part over the paddies, symbolizing warmth and the clearing of hard weather. It is often chosen for its connection to the bright days on which rice is planted and dried and its representation of hope that outlasts the rain.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Utsumi Teruhi, a Sengoku-period woman on Japanese Wikipedia (surname stripped); reading is the standard one for this bearer, confirm on the article. Kanji 照日 (to shine + sun, day), read teru-hi, both kun readings, straightforward. Samurai-household style in the source; a plain nature compound that would also sit comfortably in a commoner register.

name: Zensei
explanation: Zensei - This name means "good star". It represents a birth under a favorable sky, the hope that the Fortunes have set a kindly light over the child's road.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of two-character auspicious names (zen 'good' + sei 'star') of the kind commoner families gave in hope of luck, and we have no record of Zensei as a personal name. Kanji 善星: 善 'good, virtuous' (zen) and 星 'star' (sei), both ordinary on-readings, so a Japanese reader parses it straightforwardly, though on-on compounds of this kind are more typical of monks' and shop names than of women's register names. Commoner style, auspicious-word type; not a court name. The homophone 前世 'previous life' is worth knowing but is written with different kanji.

name: Zuihana
explanation: Zuihana means "auspicious flower" or "omen-blossom", which can suggest a child whose birth was taken for a good sign or a beauty that announces good fortune to come. People with this name may be treated as lucky charms by their neighbors and expected to bring a bright season with them.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of the flower names Edo commoner women bore (Hana, Kiku, Ume) with an auspicious prefix, and we have no record of Zuihana as a personal name. Kanji 瑞花: 瑞 'auspicious sign, omen' (zui, on-reading) and 花 'flower' (hana, kun-reading); the mixed on-kun reading is stylized - the same compound read as a word is zuika, a poetic term for snow as the 'auspicious flower' that promises a good harvest, so a Japanese reader would recognize the characters but find the reading unusual. Commoner register style with a lucky-word flourish; not a court name.

name: Fuchi
explanation: Fuchi - This name pays tribute to the Festival of Still Waters, held where a river slows into a deep pool before the autumn rains, an event that emphasizes patience, depth of feeling, and the quiet strength of what lies beneath a calm surface. People choose this name to reflect their values for composure and the kind of loyalty that runs deep without needing to be seen.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: recorded in kana (ふち) among Edo-period women's names transcribed by the Nishinomiya City Local History Museum document-reading group. The conventional kanji is 淵 (fuchi, 'deep pool in a river'), a nature word of exactly the kind Edo commoner women bore (Kiku, Matsu, Tsuru); the register itself gives no kanji. Commoner register style, suitable for any caste in this setting. The Festival of Still Waters is a Rokugani invention for the explanation.

name: Ate
explanation: Ate - This name represents nobility and preciousness, and is often chosen by those who are born into the upper ranks of a great house or who are expected to carry themselves with the dignity of the Emperor's court.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: borne by Keikoin (1666-1683), whose article on Japanese Wikipedia gives her given name as 貴姫 (Atehime), the hime honorific stripped here; she was a daughter of the Owari Tokugawa line (Tokugawa Mitsutomo) and wife of Asano Tsunanaga of Hiroshima. Kanji 貴 'noble, precious, exalted'; the reading ate is a STYLIZED name reading (the kanji is ordinarily ki or tattoi/toutoi), attested for this bearer and drawn from the classical adjective ate 'noble, refined', so it needs explaining to a modern reader. A court/high-samurai name, not a commoner register name. No notable modern association.

name: Aguri
explanation: Aguri - A name derived from the fusion of "long-lasting" and "village home", reflecting a balance between endurance and belonging. It is often embraced by those who strive for a house that stands in one place for generations.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Oto Aguri (b. 1648), wife of Makino Narisada of Sekiyado, on Japanese Wikipedia; this firms up a form previously held only from a low-confidence Sengoku name dictionary. Kanji 阿久里 as recorded: 阿 (a, 'corner, nook'), 久 (ku, 'long-lasting') and 里 (ri, 'village, home'); the alternate 安久里 substitutes 安 (a, 'peace') for the first character. Readings are regular, but both spellings are essentially ateji chosen for sound, so the combined meaning is loose. Early-Edo samurai-wife name in the everyday register; Aguri was also borne by Edo commoner women. The best-known bearer is Asano Naganori's wife Aguri (Yozeiin, 1674-1714) of the Ako incident, and Aguri survives as a rare modern given name.

name: Iwashiro
explanation: Iwashiro - This name signifies a foundation of rock that endures through the generations, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values steadfastness, an unshakeable home, and a line that will outlast its founders.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Oe Iwashiro (1744-1813), commoner-born in Kurayoshi in Hoki, consort of Prince Kan'in Sukehito and mother of Emperor Kokaku, on Japanese Wikipedia. Kanji 磐代: 磐 'great rock, bedrock' (iwa) and 代 'generation, age, in place of' (shiro, its regular kun reading); read together as 'rock for generations', and Iwashiro is also an old poetic place name (a cape in Kii sung of in the Man'yoshu), which is likely how it was chosen. A commoner-born name later carried into the court; in this setting it suits a peasant or a heimen woman who rose. No notable modern association beyond the historical bearer.

name: Ikuko
explanation: Ikuko - A name that means "fragrant child", evoking a daughter whose grace is felt the way incense is felt, quietly filling a room before anyone has turned to look.
notes: Attested pre-modern name: Ichijo Ikuko (1729-1808), wife of Tokugawa Munemoto of Mito, on Japanese Wikipedia; also Noma Ikuko (1849-1946), concubine of Kujo Michitaka and grandmother of Emperor Showa. Kanji 郁子: 郁 'fragrant, cultured, flourishing' (iku, its regular on reading) and 子 'child' (ko); the alternate spelling 幾子 uses 幾 'how many, several' (iku), a purely phonetic choice with no real sense. Court -ko name of the Edo nobility, acceptable for any caste in this setting. Ikuko remains an ordinary modern given name.

name: Gekka
explanation: Gekka chose their name in honor of the famous Kitsune Gekka, who kept a night vigil beneath the moon for seven days to guide a lost caravan home across the Fox lands.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the Edo commoner idiom of nature, plant, season and object words (the village registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Nabe, Ine), with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 月下: 月 'moon' (getsu, on-reading) and 下 'beneath' (ka), a poetic on-yomi compound that reads as the term gekka, 'under the moon', more than as a name. Commoner-flavored word-name rather than a register or court name. Gekka bijin, 'beauty under the moon', is the Japanese name for the night-blooming cereus.

name: Gyokusen
explanation: Gyokusen - Derived from the phrase "a spring as clear as jade", this name embodies the idea of purity welling up from hidden depths. It is often associated with those who offer quiet refreshment to everyone around them.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the Edo commoner idiom of nature, plant, season and object words (the village registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Nabe, Ine), with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 玉泉: 玉 'jewel, jade' (gyoku) and 泉 'spring, fountain' (sen), a plain on-yomi compound meaning 'jewel spring'. Word-name in the commoner idiom, not a register or court name. Gyokusen is real as an art name (go) of several painters, which is a different usage from a given name.

name: Gyokuha
explanation: Gyokuha - Composed of the elements "jewel" and "wave", this name symbolizes beauty that is always in motion, glittering and never still. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of grace, liveliness and a bright spirit.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the Edo commoner idiom of nature, plant, season and object words (the village registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Nabe, Ine), with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 玉波: 玉 'jewel' (gyoku) and 波 'wave' (ha), both on-readings; the compound is a stylized poetic term, 'jeweled waves', and reads more like a phrase from verse than a personal name - it would need explaining in the prose. Commoner-flavored word-name, neither register nor court.

name: Futae
explanation: Futae - With origins in the legend of the twin sisters of Twofold Ford, who each took the other's watch so that the village was never unguarded, this name evokes a sense of doubled care and steadfast devotion. It appeals to those who admire loyalty that never leaves a gap.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the Edo commoner idiom of nature, plant, season and object words (the village registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Nabe, Ine), with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 二重: 二 'two' (futa) and 重 'fold, layer' (e), kun readings giving futae, 'twofold, double', an ordinary word. Commoner-flavored word-name. Futae is borne as a modern female given name, but our sources hold no pre-modern record of it.

name: Biwako
explanation: Biwako - This name is inspired by the natural element of the loquat tree, symbolizing sweetness ripening in early summer. It is often chosen for its connection to orchards and shaded courtyards and its representation of modest, dependable fruitfulness.
notes: Not attested in our sources; built on the attested Heian and Kamakura court pattern of an auspicious plant or virtue kanji plus 子 (as in Fujiko, Matsuko), but there is no record of this specific name. Kanji 枇杷子: 枇杷 'loquat' (biwa) plus 子 'child' (ko), read straightforwardly Biwako. Court-style -ko name, acceptable for any caste here. Homophonous with Lake Biwa (琵琶湖), which uses different kanji ('lute lake') - a modern reader hears the lake first.

name: Jinju
explanation: Jinju - A name derived from the fusion of "benevolence" and "long life", reflecting a balance between kindness to others and care for oneself. It is often embraced by those who strive for a long, gentle and honorable old age.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the Edo commoner idiom of nature, plant, season and object words (the village registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Nabe, Ine), with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 仁寿: 仁 'benevolence' (jin) and 寿 'long life, felicity' (ju), an on-yomi compound. Note that the same characters are the Heian era name Ninju (851-854), so the reading Jinju is a stylized Chinese-style reading of 仁; a Japanese reader would say Ninju. Auspicious word-name rather than a register or court name.

name: Jumi
explanation: The name Jumi is associated with the famous Hundredth-Year Blessing, in which an Emperor granted a village a century of tax relief after its eldest woman danced for the court on her hundredth birthday. Those who choose this name try to embody values of long life, grace in age and joy freely given.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the Edo commoner idiom of nature, plant, season and object words (the village registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Nabe, Ine), with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 寿美: 寿 'longevity' (ju) and 美 'beauty' (mi), read with an on-reading and a kun-style name reading; the same kanji are more usually read Sumi or Kazumi as a modern name, so Jumi is a stylized reading. Auspicious word-name in the commoner idiom, not a register or court name.

name: Rokka
explanation: The name Rokka is inspired by the high passes of the northern mountains, known for their six-pointed snow crystals that lie unmelted until late spring. The name reflects the delicate perfection of the place and is often chosen by those who value purity, brevity and precise beauty.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the Edo commoner idiom of nature, plant, season and object words (the village registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Nabe, Ine), with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 六花: 六 'six' (roku, contracted to rok-) and 花 'flower' (ka), an on-yomi compound that is a real poetic word for snow, 'six-petaled flower', after the six-fold crystal. Commoner-flavored nature word, not a register or court name. Rokka survives as a brand name and confectionery name in Hokkaido.

name: Ranka
explanation: Ranka - This name pays tribute to the Orchid Viewing, an event that emphasizes refinement, patience and the quiet appreciation of rare things. People choose this name to reflect their values for cultivated taste and the worth of what blooms seldom.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the Edo commoner idiom of nature, plant, season and object words (the village registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Nabe, Ine), with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 蘭花: 蘭 'orchid' (ran) and 花 'flower, blossom' (ka), an on-yomi compound meaning 'orchid blossom'. Commoner-flavored plant-name; the orchid is one of the Four Gentlemen of ink painting, so it carries a scholarly tone. Ranka is known to modern audiences as a character name in the anime Macross Frontier.

name: Uzuki
explanation: Uzuki - This name represents the fourth month, when the deutzia blooms and the rice is sown, and is often chosen by those who are born in that month or who are expected to bring the promise of a good planting.
notes: Not attested in our sources as a personal name; the month names Yayoi and Uzuki were used as names in the Edo period, and this entry is constructed in that commoner idiom of season and calendar words. Kanji 卯月: 卯 'the Hare, fourth branch' (u) and 月 'month' (tsuki, voiced to -zuki), the classical name of the fourth lunar month. Commoner-style calendar name, not a court name. Modern audiences know Shimamura Uzuki from The Idolmaster Cinderella Girls.

name: Ushio
explanation: Ushio - This name means "tide". It represents the pull of the sea and the moon, the rhythm of coming and going that never fails, and the strength of what returns.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the Edo commoner idiom of nature, plant, season and object words (the village registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Nabe, Ine), with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 潮: a single character meaning 'tide, sea current', with the native kun reading ushio. Commoner-flavored nature word, of the kind fishing-village families might bear. In modern Japan Ushio is a real given name, mostly for men, and a surname; our pre-modern sources do not record it.

name: Wagiku
explanation: Wagiku means "native chrysanthemum" or "harmonious chrysanthemum", which can suggest a flower of one's own soil or a blossom that brings peace to a household. People with this name may be steady, homely in the best sense and quietly proud of where they come from.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the Edo commoner idiom of nature, plant, season and object words (the village registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Nabe, Ine), with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 和菊: 和 'harmony; Japanese, native' (wa) and 菊 'chrysanthemum' (kiku, voiced to -giku by rendaku), giving 'native chrysanthemum', a horticultural term. Built on Kiku, one of the commonest Edo register names, so it sits in the commoner plant-name idiom; not a court name.

name: Zoho
explanation: Zoho - A name that means "added rice ears", evoking a harvest that comes in heavier than the tally and a household whose store keeps growing.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the Edo commoner idiom of nature, plant, season and object words (the village registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Nabe, Ine), with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 増穂: 増 'increase' (zo, on-reading) and 穂 'ear of grain' (ho), an on-yomi compound that reads like a poetic or place-name term rather than a personal name; the same characters are the town name Masuho in Yamanashi, read in kun, so Zoho is a stylized reading. Commoner farming word-name, not a register or court name.

name: Zuiran
explanation: Zuiran chose their name in honor of the famous Asako Zuiran, who tended the orchid house of a provincial governor and read in a single unseasonable bloom the omen that saved the harvest.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the Edo commoner idiom of nature, plant, season and object words (the village registers carry Kiku, Matsu, Nabe, Ine), with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 瑞蘭: 瑞 'auspicious, felicitous' (zui) and 蘭 'orchid' (ran), both on-readings; the compound is a stylized poetic term, 'auspicious orchid', and reads more like an art name or a phrase from verse than a given name, which the prose should acknowledge. Commoner-flavored plant-name, neither register nor court.

name: Edano
explanation: Edano - Derived from the phrase "a branch of the old tree", this name embodies the idea of a daughter who carries her family's line onward like new growth from an established trunk. It is often associated with those who keep faith with their parents' house while making something of their own.
notes: Attested-idiom name, NOT a recorded one: built on the Edo pattern of a short stem plus the suffix 乃 (no), which registers show on names like Yaeno and Yoshino, from the stem 枝 (eda, 'branch'), a nature word of the kind Edo commoner women bore. Kanji 枝乃: 枝 'branch' (eda) + 乃 'of' (no), both ordinary readings. We have no evidence of this specific name being borne by a historical person; it is offered because the pool needed another E- name. Commoner style, fine for any caste in this setting.

name: Bien
explanation: Bien - Stemming from the word "bien", which denotes a fair garden, this name embodies the spirit of beauty tended patiently over seasons. It resonates with those who are quietly diligent, who find contentment in cultivating what is close at hand, and who believe that grace is grown rather than seized.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a two-kanji auspicious word of the kind Edo commoner registers show, with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 美園: 美 bi (beauty, fair) + 園 en (garden), read bi-en, both standard on-readings. Commoner register style rather than a court name.

name: Benno
explanation: Benno - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A well-turned word opens the gate that a hundred swords cannot", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value eloquence, tact, and the courtier's art of winning without a blade drawn.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of an auspicious stem plus the register suffix 乃 no, the pattern Edo village registers show on names like Yaeno, with no record of this specific name. Kanji 弁乃: 弁 ben (eloquence, speech, discernment) + 乃 no (of), read ben-no. Commoner register style. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Ayano
explanation: Ayano - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the weaver of Willow Ford, in which a village girl wove a bolt of twill so fine that the provincial governor mistook it for the work of a court atelier and, learning the truth, raised her whole hamlet from its tax debt. It reflects qualities such as patience, skilled hands, and the dignity of humble craft honestly done.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a stem plus the register suffix 乃 no, as Edo village registers show on Yaeno and the like, with no record of this specific name in our lists (it is common as a modern given name). Kanji 綾乃: 綾 aya (twill, figured silk) + 乃 no (of), read aya-no, standard readings. Commoner register style. The tale and Willow Ford are Rokugani inventions.

name: Akiyo
explanation: Akiyo - This name pays tribute to the Autumn Sheaf Festival, an event that emphasizes gratitude for the harvest and the passing of the fields from one generation to the next. People choose this name to reflect their values for continuity, the honoring of ancestors who worked the same land, and the quiet abundance of a season gathered in.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a stem plus the register suffix 代 yo, the pattern Edo registers show on names like Sayo, with no record of this specific name. Kanji 秋代: 秋 aki (autumn) + 代 yo (generation, era), read aki-yo, standard kun-readings. Commoner register style. The Autumn Sheaf Festival is a Rokugani invention.

name: Harue
explanation: Harue - Derived from the phrase "spring returns to the inlet", this name embodies the idea of renewal after hardship, of ice giving way and boats going out again. It is often associated with those who bring warmth and fresh beginnings to the households and villages they join.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a stem plus the register suffix 江 e, as Edo registers show on commoner women's names, with no record of this specific name in our lists (it is attested as a modern given name). Kanji 春江: 春 haru (spring) + 江 e (inlet, creek), read haru-e, standard kun-readings. Commoner register style. The phrase in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Hideno
explanation: Hideno was a deity that was said to have taught the first rice farmers to select the finest heads of grain for next year's seed after watching a sparrow choose only the fullest ears from a threshing floor.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of an auspicious stem plus the register suffix 乃 no, the pattern Edo registers show on Yaeno, with no record of this specific name. Kanji 秀乃: 秀 hide (to excel, outstanding) + 乃 no (of), read hide-no, standard readings. Commoner register style. The deity in the explanation is a Rokugani invention, a minor local Fortune, not canon.

name: Eshiko
explanation: Eshiko - Rooted in the ancient proverb "A blessing without resolve is rain on stone", this name serves as a reminder of the wisdom it contains. It is often chosen by those who value purpose, gratitude put into action, and the discipline to make good fortune bear fruit.
notes: Follows the attested Heian court pattern of auspicious kanji plus 子 ko, but there is no record of this specific name in our sources. Kanji 恵志子: 恵 e (blessing, grace) + 志 shi (will, resolve, aspiration) + 子 ko (child), read e-shi-ko, all standard readings. Court -ko style, acceptable for any caste in this setting. The proverb in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Gimi
explanation: Gimi was a deity that was said to have descended to a mountain shrine to correct the bows of the villagers after their sloppy rites had offended the spirits of the peak and brought three years of poor snowmelt.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a two-kanji auspicious word, with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 儀美: 儀 gi (ceremony, rite, proper form) + 美 mi (beauty), read gi-mi, both standard on-readings. Commoner register style. The deity in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Chiyu
explanation: Chiyu - This name means "a thousand reasons". It represents a daughter whose parents hoped she would always find cause enough to go on, whatever the year brought.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a two-kanji auspicious word, with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 千由: 千 chi (thousand) + 由 yu (reason, origin, source), read chi-yu; 千 as chi is the kun-reading used in names like Chiyo, 由 as yu is standard. Commoner register style.

name: Zuigetsu
explanation: Zuigetsu - This name pays tribute to the Vigil of the Auspicious Moon, an event that emphasizes watchfulness, omen-reading, and the reading of Lord Moon's face for the year to come. People choose this name to reflect their values for patience, attentiveness to signs, and trust that good fortune reveals itself to those who wait through the night for it.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a two-kanji auspicious word, with no record of it as a personal name, and its on-reading shape is more typical of a monastic or literary name than of a village register. Kanji 瑞月: 瑞 zui (auspicious, felicitous omen) + 月 getsu (moon), read zui-getsu, both standard on-readings. Commoner register style by tag, though the sound is unusually formal for one. The Vigil of the Auspicious Moon is a Rokugani invention.

name: Zenmu
explanation: Zenmu chose their name in honor of the famous Dragon monk Zenmu, who dreamed the location of a buried spring three nights running and led a drought-stricken village to dig where she had seen the water rise.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a two-kanji auspicious word of a monastic flavor, with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 善夢: 善 zen (good, virtuous) + 夢 mu (dream), read zen-mu, both standard on-readings. Commoner register style by tag, though the on-reading sound is closer to a monk's name. The monk Zenmu in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Kiyoe
explanation: Kiyoe - A name that means "pure inlet", evoking a sheltered stretch of clear water where a family moors its boats and a daughter is expected to be as calm and unclouded as it.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a stem plus the register suffix 江 e, as Edo registers show on commoner women's names, with no record of this specific name in our lists. Kanji 清江: 清 kiyo (pure, clear) + 江 e (inlet), read kiyo-e, standard kun-readings. Commoner register style.

name: Sumie
explanation: Sumie - Derived from the phrase "the inlet clears when the wind lies down", this name embodies the idea of a calm mind in which the truth can be seen to the bottom. It is often associated with those who keep their composure in argument and see plainly what others muddy.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a stem plus the register suffix 江 e, as Edo registers show on commoner women's names, with no record of this specific name in our lists (it is attested as a modern given name). Kanji 澄江: 澄 sumi (clear, limpid, settled) + 江 e (inlet), read sumi-e, standard readings. Commoner register style. The phrase in the explanation is a Rokugani invention.

name: Benimi
explanation: Benimi - Composed of the elements "crimson" and "beauty", this name symbolizes the vivid loveliness of safflower dye and of maple leaves at the turn of the year. It is commonly chosen for its connotations of warmth, striking presence, and a beauty that does not fade into the background.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a two-kanji auspicious word, with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 紅美: 紅 beni (crimson, rouge, safflower red) + 美 mi (beauty), read beni-mi; 紅 as beni is the standard kun-reading, 美 as mi the standard on-reading. Commoner register style.

name: Emu
explanation: Emu - This name is inspired by the ancient tale of the dreaming bride of the marsh road, in which a young wife dreamed for seven nights of a stranger's gift and, when a lost traveler at last knocked at her door, fed and sheltered him and was rewarded when he proved to be a Fortune in disguise. It reflects qualities such as generosity, faith in omens, and kindness shown before any reward is certain.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a two-kanji auspicious word, with no record of it as a personal name. Kanji 恵夢: 恵 e (blessing, grace) + 夢 mu (dream), read e-mu, both standard readings. Commoner register style. The tale in the explanation is a Rokugani invention. Note the incidental modern collision with the English bird name, which has no bearing on the Rokugani name.

name: Etsu
explanation: Etsu - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the harvest-dance performed at village shrines, this name represents the joy of a community moving together in thanks. It is often chosen by those who appreciate delight shared openly and without pride and have a deep respect for the elders who teach each year's children the steps.
notes: Attested pre-modern commoner name: a dated bearer is Endo Etsu (1814), of a village-headman family in Shimosa, recorded in the kotobank name dictionary and the Nishinomiya document collection. Kanji 悦: etsu (joy, delight), a single-character name read with its standard on-reading. Commoner register style; single-kanji names of this kind are typical of Edo village registers. The harvest-dance in the explanation is a generic Rokugani village custom, not a named real-world form.

name: Hiroko
explanation: Hiroko - This name signifies a broad and generous spirit, a heart with room in it for many, and may suggest that the one who chooses it values hospitality, open-handedness, and a wide view that does not narrow under pressure.
notes: Follows the attested Heian court pattern of auspicious kanji plus 子 ko, but there is no record of this specific name in our pre-modern sources. Kanji 広子: 広 hiro (broad, wide) + 子 ko (child), read hiro-ko, standard readings. Court -ko style, acceptable for any caste in this setting. Extremely common as a modern given name, which is the main association a modern reader will have.

name: Gyokuko
explanation: The name Gyokuko is inspired by the Jewel Terraces, a stretch of paddies on the slopes above a mountain lake known for their clear water and the way they shine like a string of green gems at planting. The name reflects the polished, precious quality of the place and is often chosen by those who value refinement, worth proven by patient labor, and beauty in orderly things.
notes: Follows the attested Heian court pattern of auspicious kanji plus 子 ko, but there is no record of this specific name in our sources. Kanji 玉子: 玉 gyoku (jewel, jade) + 子 ko (child), read gyoku-ko using the on-reading of 玉; this is a stylized court-style reading, since the same two characters are read tamago (egg) in everyday modern usage, a collision worth knowing before using the name aloud. Court -ko style, acceptable for any caste in this setting. The Jewel Terraces are a Rokugani invention.

name: Gakuyo
explanation: The name Gakuyo is inspired by the high peaks of the Dragon lands, known for their monasteries, their thin cold air, and the generations of hermits who have watched the Empire from above. The name reflects the enduring, unmoving character of the place and is often chosen by those who value steadfastness, long perspective, and loyalty that outlasts a single lifetime.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a stem plus the register suffix 代 yo, as Edo registers show on names like Sayo, with no record of this specific name. Kanji 岳代: 岳 gaku (mountain peak) + 代 yo (generation), read gaku-yo, mixing the on-reading of 岳 with the kun-reading of 代, which is a somewhat stylized combination. Commoner register style.

name: Nagi
explanation: Nagi - Drawing inspiration from the traditional art form of the coastal boat-song, sung by fishing crews to keep the oars in time on a windless sea, this name represents the calm in which such songs carry farthest. It is often chosen by those who appreciate stillness and steady rhythm and have a deep respect for the singers who hold a crew together through the long flat hours.
notes: Not attested in our sources; constructed in the pre-modern idiom of a single-character nature word of the kind Edo commoners bore, with no record of it as a personal name in our lists (it is used as a modern given name). Kanji 凪: nagi (calm, a windless lull at sea), a native Japanese character read with its standard kun-reading. Commoner register style. The boat-song in the explanation is a generic Rokugani custom, not a named real-world form.
